course.title: Mathematical Foundations for Data Science
course.description:
The mathematics you need before machine learning, in three connected parts: **Linear Algebra** (linear systems, matrices, determinants, eigenvalues, vector spaces, linear mappings), **Calculus and Optimization** (functions, derivatives, the chain rule, partial derivatives, gradients, gradient descent) and **Probability and Statistics** (conditional probability, Bayes' rule, random variables, distributions, expectation, variance, joint distributions, sampling, estimation and confidence intervals).

15 topics · about 45 hours (15 class hours + 30 hours of independent study). Each topic has worked examples, practice questions with feedback on the exact misconception behind a wrong answer, and flashcards for spaced review. Lecture notes and slides for every part are attached as PDFs.

misconceptions.name: Treats a product, power or function of the unknowns as linear
misconceptions.description: Calls an equation linear because it is an equation in x and y, even though an unknown is squared, multiplied by another unknown, or placed inside a function such as eˣ. An equation is linear only if each unknown appears to the first power, multiplied by a fixed number, and is only added to other terms.

misconceptions.name: Writes the augmented matrix with a wrong sign or column order
misconceptions.description: Transcribes a system into [A | b] with a sign changed, or with the columns in a different order from the declared unknowns. The first columns must hold the coefficients of x, y, … in that order and the last column must hold the right-hand sides with their signs.

misconceptions.name: Believes an operation that destroys information is an elementary row operation
misconceptions.description: Thinks that multiplying a row by zero, replacing a row by a copy of another, or swapping variable columns preserves the solution set. Only three operations are safe: swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero number, and add a multiple of one row to another. Each of these can be undone; the faulty ones cannot.

misconceptions.name: Carries out a row replacement incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Applies R2 ← R2 − 3R1 to only part of the row: leaves the right-hand side unchanged, forgets that the first entry changes too, or adds where it should subtract. A row operation acts on every entry of the row, including the entry after the bar.

misconceptions.name: Misreads a row of zeros in an augmented matrix
misconceptions.description: Reads a row [0 0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0 as harmless or as meaning infinitely many solutions, or reads the row [0 0 0 | 0] as a contradiction. The first says 0 = c, which is impossible; the second says 0 = 0, which is always true.

misconceptions.name: Checks or substitutes carelessly
misconceptions.description: Back-substitutes with a missing coefficient (x = 7 − y instead of x = 7 − 2y) or verifies a candidate in only some equations. A vector is a solution only if it satisfies every equation of the system.

misconceptions.name: Loses a sign or a variable when writing the general solution
misconceptions.description: Moves a free-variable term across the equals sign without changing its sign (x1 + 2x3 = 3 gives x1 = 3 − 2t, not 3 + 2t), or ignores that the free variable also appears in the other equations. Spanning vectors proposed for a solution set must themselves satisfy the equations.

misconceptions.name: Assumes a system with a parameter behaves the same for every value
misconceptions.description: Treats a system containing a parameter a as having one type of solution for all a. Elimination produces factors such as (a − 2); at the value that makes such a factor vanish, a pivot disappears and the number of solutions changes (unique, none or infinitely many).

misconceptions.name: Misjudges how many solutions a system has
misconceptions.description: Counts solutions by the number of unknowns, thinks a homogeneous system can have no solution or only the zero solution regardless of shape, or thinks fewer equations than unknowns can still give a unique solution. Uniqueness needs a pivot in every variable column; if there are more unknowns than pivots, a consistent system has infinitely many solutions.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up the shape rules for addition and multiplication
misconceptions.description: Believes A + B is defined whenever the shapes are 'similar' (same number of rows, or same number of entries), or gives the shape of AB as swapped or as the inner dimensions. Addition needs identical shapes. For multiplication the inner dimensions must agree and the result has the outer dimensions: (m × k)(k × n) is m × n.

misconceptions.name: Applies a scalar to only some entries or changes its sign
misconceptions.description: Multiplies only the diagonal (or one row) of a matrix by a scalar, or uses +c instead of −c. In cA every entry is multiplied by c.

misconceptions.name: Pairs the wrong entries in a matrix product
misconceptions.description: Multiplies matching entries (entrywise product) or uses the wrong row or column. The entry (AB)ij is the sum of products of row i of A with column j of B.

misconceptions.name: Assumes AB = BA
misconceptions.description: Treats matrix multiplication like multiplication of numbers and swaps the factors freely. In general AB ≠ BA, and one of the products may not even be defined.

misconceptions.name: Transposes incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Leaves the matrix unchanged, reverses the entries, rotates it, or forgets to transpose when combining rules. The transpose turns row i into column i, so an m × n matrix becomes n × m.

misconceptions.name: Misremembers the 2 × 2 inverse formula
misconceptions.description: Forgets the factor 1/(ad − bc), keeps the signs of the off-diagonal entries, or does not swap the diagonal entries. For [[a,b],[c,d]] the inverse is 1/(ad − bc) · [[d, −b],[−c, a]].

misconceptions.name: Keeps the original order when transposing or inverting a product
misconceptions.description: Writes (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ or (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹, or treats the inverse of a sum as the sum of inverses. Both rules reverse the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

misconceptions.name: Mishandles a scalar factor inside an inverse
misconceptions.description: Writes (cA)⁻¹ = cA⁻¹ instead of c⁻¹A⁻¹, or drops the scalar altogether. Inverting reciprocates the scalar.

misconceptions.name: Solves a matrix equation by multiplying on the wrong side or by the wrong matrix
misconceptions.description: In AXB = I multiplies by A and B instead of A⁻¹ and B⁻¹, or multiplies both factors on the same side. To isolate X you must multiply on the left by A⁻¹ and on the right by B⁻¹, and the order matters.

misconceptions.name: Cancels a matrix factor as if it were a nonzero number
misconceptions.description: From AB = AC concludes B = C. This is valid only if A is invertible (multiply by A⁻¹); otherwise B and C can differ.

misconceptions.name: Uses the wrong formula for a 2 × 2 determinant
misconceptions.description: Adds the diagonal products, or takes only one product, instead of computing ad − bc. The determinant is the main-diagonal product minus the other-diagonal product.

misconceptions.name: Forgets the checkerboard sign or deletes the wrong row and column
misconceptions.description: Takes the minor as the cofactor, or deletes the wrong row or column when forming the minor. The cofactor is Cij = (−1)^(i+j) · Mij, where Mij comes from deleting row i and column j.

misconceptions.name: Does not take the product of the diagonal of a triangular matrix
misconceptions.description: Adds the diagonal entries, drops a sign, or thinks an entry of 0 anywhere makes the determinant 0. For a triangular matrix det A is the product of the diagonal entries, signs included.

misconceptions.name: Misjudges how row operations change the determinant
misconceptions.description: Forgets that a row swap changes the sign, that scaling a row by c multiplies the determinant by c, or thinks that adding a multiple of one row to another changes the determinant. Replacement leaves it unchanged.

misconceptions.name: Treats the determinant as if it were linear
misconceptions.description: Writes det(A + B) = det A + det B, or det(cA) = c·det A. The determinant is multiplicative (det AB = det A · det B), and scaling an n × n matrix by c multiplies the determinant by cⁿ.

misconceptions.name: Misapplies a determinant rule for inverses, products or the adjoint
misconceptions.description: Uses the wrong sign or exponent in det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, det(A²) = (det A)², det(Aᵀ) = det A, or det(adj A) = (det A)ⁿ⁻¹. A single wrong sign changes the final answer.

misconceptions.name: Thinks det A = 0 means Ax = b never has a solution
misconceptions.description: Confuses 'A is not invertible' with 'the system is inconsistent'. If det A = 0 then Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many, depending on b.

misconceptions.name: Pairs an eigenvector with an eigenvalue it does not belong to
misconceptions.description: Chooses an eigenvalue or eigenvector without checking Av = λv for that pair. A vector can be an eigenvector for one eigenvalue and still fail the equation for another.

misconceptions.name: Adds conditions to the definition of an eigenvector or eigenvalue
misconceptions.description: Requires the eigenvalue to be nonzero, the eigenvector to have length one, or all its coordinates to be nonzero. The definition needs only v ≠ 0 and Av = λv; λ = 0 is allowed and happens exactly when A is singular.

misconceptions.name: Misreads the eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix
misconceptions.description: Invents an eigenvalue, drops a sign, or takes absolute values. The eigenvalues of a diagonal (or triangular) matrix are exactly its diagonal entries, with their signs.

misconceptions.name: Gets the eigenvalue of A⁻¹ wrong
misconceptions.description: Thinks A⁻¹ has the same eigenvalue as A, or its negative, or its square. If Av = λv with λ ≠ 0 then A⁻¹v = (1/λ)v.

misconceptions.name: Orders the diagonal entries differently from the eigenvector columns
misconceptions.description: Builds P from eigenvectors but writes the eigenvalues in D in another order. In A = PDP⁻¹ the j-th diagonal entry of D must be the eigenvalue of the j-th column of P.

misconceptions.name: Misjudges when a matrix is diagonalizable
misconceptions.description: Thinks a repeated eigenvalue always rules out diagonalization (or always allows it), or counts eigenvalues instead of independent eigenvectors. A is diagonalizable over ℝ exactly when it has n linearly independent real eigenvectors.

misconceptions.name: Mishandles powers or polynomials of a matrix
misconceptions.description: Slips when computing an entry of Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ (wrong factor, wrong row or column of P or P⁻¹), or forgets that p(A)v = p(λ)v, so that (for a diagonalizable A) the kernel of p(A) is spanned by the eigenvectors whose eigenvalues are roots of p.

misconceptions.name: Slips in componentwise, pointwise or linear-combination arithmetic
misconceptions.description: Subtracts instead of adds, multiplies instead of adds, loses the sign of a subtracted function, or applies a negative coefficient to only one coordinate. Vector spaces add componentwise (or pointwise for functions).

misconceptions.name: Confuses the additive identity with the multiplicative identity
misconceptions.description: In a function space picks the constant function 1, or another function, as the zero vector. The zero vector is the function that is 0 for every t, because it is the only one that leaves every function unchanged under pointwise addition.

misconceptions.name: Misuses the test T(0) = 0
misconceptions.description: Does not know that every linear map sends 0 to 0 (so T(0) ≠ 0 proves non-linearity), computes T(0) incorrectly, or treats T(0) = 0 as enough to prove linearity. T(0) = 0 is necessary but not sufficient.

misconceptions.name: Builds the standard matrix incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Writes the images T(e1), T(e2), … as rows instead of columns, swaps the columns, or loses a sign. The standard matrix is A = [T(e1) … T(en)]: the j-th column is the image of ej.

misconceptions.name: Believes a map such as a translation, absolute value or square is linear
misconceptions.description: Treats a map as linear because it 'looks simple'. A translation fails T(0) = 0; squaring fails additivity; the absolute value fails homogeneity for negative scalars.

misconceptions.name: Applies T instead of T⁻¹, or solves an operator equation carelessly
misconceptions.description: To invert a linear map applies the map itself, forgets to reciprocate the eigenvalues, or ignores that a constant such as f(0) is itself unknown. The inverse of T undoes T.

misconceptions.name: Applies only part of the subspace test
misconceptions.description: Checks that a set contains 0, or that it is closed under addition, and stops. A subset is a subspace only if it contains 0 and is closed under both addition and scalar multiplication.

misconceptions.name: Misapplies the logarithm rules
misconceptions.description: Treats the logarithm of a sum as a sum of logarithms (ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b), or mixes up the product and power rules, for example writing ln(2e³) as 3 ln 2 or as 6. The identities ln(uv) = ln u + ln v, ln(u/v) = ln u − ln v and ln(uᶜ) = c ln u apply to products, quotients and powers only; a sum inside a logarithm has no such rule.

misconceptions.name: Forgets to reverse an inequality
misconceptions.description: Multiplies or divides both sides of an inequality by a negative number without reversing the sign, or loses track of the direction when the inner function is decreasing (3 − 2x falls as x grows). The solution set then lies on the wrong side of the boundary.

misconceptions.name: Misreads a domain or a range
misconceptions.description: Gets a domain or range wrong by including an endpoint the function never reaches (a logarithm whose argument is 0, or the infimum of e^u), by ignoring a vertical shift, or by ignoring a restriction such as x ≤ 0 when inverting a function. The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of values actually taken.

misconceptions.name: Confuses probability, odds and log-odds
misconceptions.description: Inverts the sigmoid with the probability p instead of the odds p/(1 − p), forgets the logarithm, or extrapolates probabilities when it is the log-odds that are affine in x for a model p = σ(b + wx).

misconceptions.name: Sets up an exponential equation with the wrong ratio
misconceptions.description: Builds the growth equation from the wrong quantity (the relative increase 3/5 instead of the growth factor 8/5) or inverts the ratio when solving e^(kt) = c for k or t.

misconceptions.name: Drops a link of the chain rule
misconceptions.description: Differentiates only the outer or only the inner function of a composition: d/dx e^(3x−1) = e^(3x−1), d/dx ln(2 + e^(3x)) = 1/(2 + e^(3x)), or omits ∂r/∂w = x in the gradient of a squared residual. Every stage of the computation contributes one factor.

misconceptions.name: Wrong derivative of the logarithm
misconceptions.description: Believes (ln x)′ = x, or differentiates ln u as u, or as 1/x without the factor u′. The derivative of ln u is u′/u: the reciprocal of the argument times the derivative of the argument.

misconceptions.name: Treats 0/0 as an answer
misconceptions.description: Substitutes into a quotient, gets 0/0, and concludes that the limit is 0, does not exist, or equals some other number. A limit looks at x near a (with x ≠ a), so a common factor can be cancelled before taking the limit.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up value, limit, continuity and differentiability
misconceptions.description: Confuses f(a), lim f, continuity and differentiability: believes a corner such as |x| is differentiable (or discontinuous), that continuity implies differentiability, that equal function values at the join of two pieces suffice for a derivative, or that equal values and slopes guarantee a second derivative.

misconceptions.name: Confuses a rate with a change
misconceptions.description: Gives the slope instead of the change in the output (forgets to multiply by Δx), the total change instead of the average rate (forgets to divide by Δx), the derivative at one end instead of the average over an interval, or the exact change when the first-order estimate f′(a)·Δx was asked for.

misconceptions.name: Slips in a basic differentiation rule
misconceptions.description: Misapplies a basic rule: drops the exponent factor of the power rule (3x⁴ → 3x³), leaves x in the derivative of a linear term (−2x → −2x), treats e^u like a power (derivative u·e^u), or differentiates a product as f′g′.

misconceptions.name: Misjudges a local approximation
misconceptions.description: Misreads how complete or how accurate an approximation is: stops at the tangent line when the second-order term was asked for, drops the ½ or the sign of the curvature term, or treats a forward or backward difference quotient as exact (or as accurate as a centered one).

misconceptions.name: Does not hold the other variables fixed
misconceptions.description: Mishandles 'hold the other variables fixed' when taking a partial derivative: differentiates with respect to the wrong variable, treats a term that contains the variable as a constant, keeps the variable where it should have disappeared, or substitutes the point's coordinates before differentiating.

misconceptions.name: Mishandles the directional derivative
misconceptions.description: Computes D_u F = ∇F · u incorrectly: does not normalise the direction to a unit vector, flips a sign, and reports ‖g‖² instead of ‖g‖ as the steepest rate.

misconceptions.name: Thinks the gradient points downhill
misconceptions.description: Takes ∇F as the direction of steepest decrease, or believes that a direction orthogonal to ∇F decreases F. The gradient is the direction of steepest ascent; −∇F is steepest descent; directions orthogonal to ∇F change F only at second order.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up residual and loss conventions
misconceptions.description: Confuses the prediction with the residual, the sign of the residual (ŷ − y: positive means overprediction), or the scale of the loss: sum of squares, MSE, half-MSE, mean absolute error. These change signs and factors of 2 in the loss and in its gradient.

misconceptions.name: Assumes partial derivatives determine every directional derivative
misconceptions.description: Believes that if all partial derivatives exist at a point, the function is differentiable there and every directional derivative equals ∇F · u. Partial derivatives describe only the coordinate slices; a function can have zero partials and still change along a diagonal.

misconceptions.name: Checks only one stationarity equation
misconceptions.description: Declares a point stationary, or solves for unknown residuals, using only one of the gradient's equations (for instance 'the mean residual is zero') and ignoring the equations for the other parameters. ∇L = 0 means every component vanishes.

misconceptions.name: Moves with the gradient instead of against it
misconceptions.description: Updates with x + ηg (or mis-signs one component of −ηg), so the iterate climbs the loss. Gradient descent is x_{k+1} = x_k − η·g_k: subtract the gradient, including its sign for negative components.

misconceptions.name: Misstates the first-order condition
misconceptions.description: Believes a minimiser must have L = 0 or ∇L = 0 everywhere, that every stationary point is a minimum (x³ at 0 is neither a minimum nor a maximum, −x² at 0 is a maximum), or treats a point with nonzero slope as stationary.

misconceptions.name: Assumes the minimiser is unique, interior or global
misconceptions.description: Takes the first stationary point or a local minimum as the global minimum, ignores boundary candidates on a closed interval, or assumes that a least-squares problem always has a unique minimiser (or reaches zero loss).

misconceptions.name: Misjudges the size of the learning rate
misconceptions.description: Gets the effect of η wrong: does not rescale η when the loss is rescaled (MSE versus half-MSE), believes a larger η is always faster, picks a rate that suits only one curvature direction, or confuses the best step along a ray with a step that returns the loss to its starting value.

misconceptions.name: Confuses the stopping tests
misconceptions.description: Treats a small step length or a small change in the loss as proof of stationarity. The step length η‖g‖ is small whenever η is tiny, even when ‖g‖ is large; only ‖g‖ ≤ ε tests approximate stationarity directly.

misconceptions.name: Writing an event as a number instead of a set of outcomes
misconceptions.description: Answers a question about an event with a count or a value (such as {0, 1, 2} or the number 1) instead of the set of outcomes that make it happen. An event is a subset of the sample space; the number of heads is a random variable, which is a different object.

misconceptions.name: Adding probabilities without subtracting the overlap
misconceptions.description: Uses P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) for events that overlap. The outcomes in A ∩ B are counted in both P(A) and P(B), so the sum is too large unless the events are disjoint.

misconceptions.name: Wrong or missing denominator in a conditional probability
misconceptions.description: Reports P(A ∩ B), a product of probabilities, or the probability of the evidence itself instead of dividing P(A ∩ B) by the probability of the conditioning event. Conditioning rescales the shared probability so that the conditioning event has probability 1.

misconceptions.name: Treating independent and mutually exclusive as the same thing
misconceptions.description: Believes that events that cannot happen together are independent, or that independent events cannot happen together. Disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent: if one occurs, the other has probability 0.

misconceptions.name: Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A)
misconceptions.description: Treats the probability of the evidence given the hypothesis as the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence (for example, sensitivity as the chance of disease after a positive test). The two conditionals have different denominators and are equal only when P(A) = P(B).

misconceptions.name: Branches not weighted and summed in the law of total probability
misconceptions.description: When a probability or a mean is built from conditional pieces, adds them, takes a plain average, or keeps a single branch instead of weighting each piece by the probability of its condition and summing over the whole partition.

misconceptions.name: Using the wrong event when the complement is needed
misconceptions.description: Computes the probability of the event itself (or of its complement alone) when the question asks about the intersection with a complement, such as P(Aᶜ ∩ B). The complement changes which part of the sample space is being intersected.

misconceptions.name: Using only one of two independent pieces of evidence
misconceptions.description: When two conditionally independent signals both occur, updates on only one of them. Each independent signal multiplies the likelihood ratio, so two flags give much stronger evidence than one.

misconceptions.name: Misreading what a random variable is
misconceptions.description: Thinks a random variable is a probability assignment, must have equally likely values, or must take a different value for every outcome. A random variable is a fixed function from outcomes to real numbers; different outcomes may share a value and the values need not be equally likely.

misconceptions.name: Treating a density value as a probability
misconceptions.description: Reads the height of a density f(x0) as the probability of the value x0, or assumes a density can never exceed 1. For a continuous variable every single point has probability 0; probabilities are areas under the density.

misconceptions.name: Errors in standardizing a normal variable or reading its cumulative probability
misconceptions.description: Divides by the variance instead of the standard deviation, forgets to subtract the mean, adds it, or reads Φ(z) as the probability of an interval. A probability between two points is Φ(upper) − Φ(lower), and N(μ, σ²) uses the variance as its second parameter.

misconceptions.name: Assembling the binomial probability incorrectly
misconceptions.description: Drops the binomial coefficient, swaps the roles of p and 1 − p, uses the wrong number of successes, or reports p itself as the probability of k successes. P(K = k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 − p)^(n − k) needs all three parts.

misconceptions.name: Mistakes when finding the density of a transformed variable
misconceptions.description: Forgets to scale by the derivative (the factor 1/|a| for U = aX + b), ignores that a decreasing transformation reverses the inequality, or assumes the transformed density is constant. The safe route is to find the CDF of the new variable first and differentiate.

misconceptions.name: Mixing up the uniform formulas
misconceptions.description: Uses the wrong ratio for a uniform probability (the interval is compared with the support, not with 1 or with the half-width) or forgets the division by 12 in (b − a)²/12 for the variance.

misconceptions.name: Wrong variance for a Bernoulli variable
misconceptions.description: Gives p, p² or 1 − p as the variance of a Bernoulli(p) variable. The variance is p(1 − p), because X² = X for a 0/1 variable gives E(X²) − p² = p − p².

misconceptions.name: Reporting a raw moment as the variance
misconceptions.description: Gives E(X) or E(X²) as the variance. The variance is the second central moment, E(X²) − [E(X)]², so the squared mean must be subtracted from the raw second moment.

misconceptions.name: Applying linear rules to a variance
misconceptions.description: Writes V(aX + b) = aV(X) + b, or V(aX) = aV(X). The shift b does not affect the spread and the scale factor enters squared: V(aX + b) = a²V(X).

misconceptions.name: Mixing up a distribution's parameter with its mean, variance, scale or rate
misconceptions.description: Assigns the wrong moment to a named distribution: takes the square root or square of λ for a Poisson variable, uses the variance as the scale or the reciprocal of the scale for an exponential, or swaps the mean and the variance.

misconceptions.name: Ignoring the offset in E[(X − c)²]
misconceptions.description: Treats E[(X − c)²] as the variance alone or as the squared offset alone. For a constant c the expected squared distance is V(X) + [E(X) − c]², the variance plus the squared difference between the mean and c.

misconceptions.name: Thinking linearity of expectation needs independence
misconceptions.description: Believes E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) holds only when X and Y are independent. Linearity of expectation holds for any random variables with finite means; independence is needed for the variance of a sum, not for its mean.

misconceptions.name: Getting a marginal distribution by summing over the wrong variable or by dividing
misconceptions.description: To find the marginal of X, sums over x, divides by the marginal of Y, or multiplies by it. A marginal of X keeps x fixed and sums the joint probabilities over every possible value of the other variable.

misconceptions.name: Confusing zero covariance with independence
misconceptions.description: Believes that Cov(X, Y) = 0 (or zero correlation) implies independence, or reverses the implication. Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance only rules out a linear relationship, so dependent variables can be uncorrelated.

misconceptions.name: Misidentifying what a conditional expectation is
misconceptions.description: Treats E(X | Y = y) as a probability, as the random variable Y, or as the mean of Y. For a fixed y it is a number: the mean of X computed from the conditional distribution. E(X | Y) is a function of the random Y, so it is itself random.

misconceptions.name: Using a joint or marginal quantity where a conditional one is needed
misconceptions.description: Reports a joint probability, a marginal probability, or the joint density as if it were a conditional probability or density. A conditional distribution divides the joint by the marginal of the conditioning variable so that it sums or integrates to 1.

misconceptions.name: Forgetting the covariance term (or its sign) in the variance of a combination
misconceptions.description: Computes V(aX + bY) as a²V(X) + b²V(Y) when X and Y are dependent, or gets the sign of the covariance term wrong. The general formula is a²V(X) + b²V(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y).

misconceptions.name: Reading association as cause
misconceptions.description: Interprets a nonzero covariance or correlation in a joint distribution as evidence that one variable causes the other. A joint table describes how the variables vary together under the model; it does not identify a causal effect.

misconceptions.name: Using the standard deviation of one observation as the standard error of the mean
misconceptions.description: Reports σ (or s) as the uncertainty of the sample mean. The standard error of X̄ is σ/√n: it describes how much the sample mean varies across repeated samples, not how much individual observations vary.

misconceptions.name: Wrong dependence of the standard error on the sample size
misconceptions.description: Divides σ by n instead of √n, takes the wrong root, or believes the standard error stays the same or grows when n increases. Because SE = σ/√n, multiplying n by 4 divides the standard error by 2.

misconceptions.name: Calling a fixed population parameter random
misconceptions.description: Says that μ, σ², or p varies from sample to sample, or that a statistic such as X̄ is fixed. In the frequentist model the parameters are fixed (though unknown) and the statistics are random before the sample is observed.

misconceptions.name: Misstating what the central limit theorem or the law of large numbers says
misconceptions.description: Claims that the CLT makes the individual observations normal, makes X̄ exactly normal for every n, or that it is the statement that X̄ converges to μ. The CLT is about the shape of the distribution of the standardized sample mean as n grows; the law of large numbers is about X̄ concentrating at μ.

misconceptions.name: Confusing the sampling distribution with the distribution of the data in one sample
misconceptions.description: Treats the sampling distribution of a statistic as a histogram of the observed values within a single sample. A sampling distribution describes the values a statistic would take across repeated samples from the same model.

misconceptions.name: Dividing by n instead of n − 1 for the sample variance (or the reverse)
misconceptions.description: Computes the sample variance S² with divisor n (or does not divide at all) when an unbiased estimate is wanted, or claims the normal-model MLE with divisor n is unbiased. S² uses n − 1; the maximum-likelihood estimator uses n and is biased downward, by the factor (n − 1)/n.

misconceptions.name: Reading unbiasedness as 'no error' or 'no variance'
misconceptions.description: Believes that an unbiased estimator has zero variance, zero MSE, or is equal to the parameter in every sample. Unbiasedness says only that the average of the estimator over repeated samples equals the parameter.

misconceptions.name: Misinterpreting what a confidence level says
misconceptions.description: Reads '95% confidence' as a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies in the one interval already computed, as the share of observations inside the interval, or as a guarantee that exactly 95 of any 100 intervals cover the parameter. The level describes the long-run coverage of the procedure.

misconceptions.name: Wrong critical value or a missing critical value in a confidence interval
misconceptions.description: Uses the standard error alone as the margin of error, uses 1.96 when the variance is unknown and a t critical value is needed, or mixes up which quantile goes with the confidence level. The margin of error is the critical value times the standard error.

misconceptions.name: Ignoring the squared bias in the mean squared error
misconceptions.description: Reports the variance of a biased estimator as its MSE, forgets to square the bias, or reports the MSE of a different estimator. MSE = variance + (bias)².

misconceptions.name: Reversing the efficiency ratio or the optimal weights
misconceptions.description: Inverts the ratio defining relative efficiency, picks the less precise estimator as the better one, or gives more weight to the noisier estimator when combining two independent unbiased estimators. The optimal weights are proportional to the inverse variances.

misconceptions.name: Errors in setting up the method of moments or maximum likelihood
misconceptions.description: Equates the parameter itself (rather than the population moment) with the sample mean, takes the largest observation as a moment estimate, flips successes and failures in a Bernoulli likelihood, or assumes that the two methods must give the same answer.

misconceptions.name: Picking the smallest eigenvalue
misconceptions.description: Treats the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue as the direction of maximum variance, or mixes up which eigenvalue measures how much spread lies along its eigenvector.

misconceptions.name: Reading the direction off the diagonal
misconceptions.description: Assumes the direction of maximum variance is a coordinate axis, or that equal variances mean no preferred direction, ignoring the off-diagonal covariance.

misconceptions.name: Wrong sign in the update
misconceptions.description: Adds the gradient instead of subtracting it, or subtracts without multiplying by the learning rate.

misconceptions.name: Slipping on a partial derivative
misconceptions.description: Differentiates one coordinate with the wrong rule (for example $3w_2$ instead of $6w_2$) when assembling the gradient.

misconceptions.name: Confusing a function with its derivative
misconceptions.description: Reports $\sigma(0)$ (the value) when asked for $\sigma'(0)$ (the slope).

misconceptions.name: Dropping the denominator or the prior
misconceptions.description: Reports the joint probability (numerator of Bayes' rule) or the prior as if it were the posterior.

misconceptions.name: Reversing the conditional
misconceptions.description: Treats $P(\text{word}\mid\text{spam})$ as if it were $P(\text{spam}\mid\text{word})$ or computes a ratio that mixes the two.

misconceptions.name: Probability statement about a fixed interval
misconceptions.description: Says there is a $95\%$ probability that $\mu$ is inside this particular computed interval.

misconceptions.name: Standard deviation instead of standard error
misconceptions.description: Uses $\sigma$ (spread of individual observations) where the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ (spread of the sample mean) belongs.

misconceptions.name: Zero covariance means independence
misconceptions.description: Believes uncorrelated variables are independent.

feedbackTemplates.body: A linear equation may contain only terms of the form (number) × (unknown). A product such as xy, a power such as x², or a function such as eˣ or sin x makes the equation nonlinear, no matter how simple it looks. Test each term: is it a fixed number times a single unknown? If yes for every term, the equation is linear.

Read the system equation by equation: column 1 is always the coefficient of the first unknown, column 2 of the second, and the last column after the bar holds the right-hand sides. Check every entry against its equation, signs included; swapping columns changes which unknown each column belongs to, so it changes the system.

A row operation is safe only if you can undo it. Multiplying a row by 0 or overwriting it with a copy of another row throws an equation away, so you cannot get it back, and the solution set can grow. Swapping variable columns relabels the unknowns, which changes the system. Stick to the three legal operations: swap rows, scale a row by c ≠ 0, add a multiple of one row to another.

A row operation acts on the whole row, the right-hand side included. For R2 ← R2 − 3R1 compute every entry of the new row 2 as (old entry of row 2) − 3 × (entry of row 1 in the same column), then keep row 1 unchanged. If the entry in the pivot column does not become 0, something went wrong.

Translate the row back into an equation. [0 0 0 | 4] says 0·x + 0·y + 0·z = 4, that is 0 = 4, which no values of the unknowns can satisfy, so the system is inconsistent. Only a row [0 0 0 | 0] (the equation 0 = 0) is harmless. The right-hand entry decides.

A solution must satisfy all equations at once. Substitute the candidate into every equation, not just the first one, and keep the coefficients when you back-substitute: in x + 2y = 7 with y = 2, the term is 2y = 4, so x = 3. Several wrong answers satisfy one equation and fail another.

Solve each pivot equation for its basic variable. From x1 + 2x3 = 3 and x3 = t you get x1 = 3 − 2t: the term 2t moves to the right with its sign flipped. Then substitute your final family back into every original equation for a few values of t. A correct general solution passes for all t.

After elimination, look at every entry that you would need to divide by. Where it contains the parameter, such as (a − 2)y = 0, split into cases: if the factor is nonzero you can divide and get a pivot; if it is zero the pivot is lost and you must read the row again (0 = 0 means a free variable, 0 = c ≠ 0 means no solution). Then check each special value separately.

Count pivots. A unique solution needs a pivot in every variable column, so you need at least as many equations as unknowns. If a system has more unknowns than equations and is consistent, a free variable exists and there are infinitely many solutions. A homogeneous system Ax = 0 is always consistent (x = 0 works), so with more unknowns than equations it has infinitely many solutions.

Write the shapes side by side. For A + B the two shapes must be identical, so a 2 × 3 matrix needs a 2 × 3 partner. For AB write (m × k)(k × n): the two inner numbers must match, and the result takes the outer numbers, m × n. Do this check before computing a single entry.

Scalar multiplication is entry by entry: (cA)ij = c·aij for every i and j, zeros included. For −2A multiply each entry by −2, so −3 becomes 6 and 2 becomes −4. Check that no entry has been skipped and that no sign has been lost.

(AB)ij is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: add the products ai1·b1j + ai2·b2j + … . Multiplying matching entries (as numpy's * does) is a different operation. Write out which row and which column you are using before you multiply.

Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Taking A = [[1,2],[0,1]] and B = [[2,0],[1,3]], AB has first row (4, 6) but BA has first row (2, 4). The order of the factors tells you which transformation acts first, so always keep it.

The transpose turns rows into columns: row 1 of A becomes column 1 of Aᵀ, row 2 becomes column 2, and so on. The shape changes from m × n to n × m, and (Aᵀ)ij = aji. Check the shape first, then fill in column by column from the rows of A.

For a 2 × 2 matrix swap the two diagonal entries, change the sign of the two off-diagonal entries, and divide everything by ad − bc. Always verify by multiplying A by your answer: you should get the identity. If the upper-right entry of the product is not 0, a sign is wrong.

Transposes and inverses of a product reverse the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. Think of putting on socks (A) then shoes (B): to undo it you remove the shoes first. Also, there is no rule for the inverse of a sum: (A + B)⁻¹ is generally not A⁻¹ + B⁻¹.
The inverse of cA undoes multiplication by c, so it contains 1/c: (cA)⁻¹ = (1/c)·A⁻¹. Combine this with (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ step by step and check by multiplying your answer with the original matrix.

To isolate X in AXB = I, multiply on the left by A⁻¹ and on the right by B⁻¹: X = A⁻¹·I·B⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹. Do not multiply by A or B themselves, and do not swap the sides. Verify by computing AXB and checking that you get I.

You may cancel A from AB = AC only by multiplying both sides by A⁻¹, which needs A to be invertible. If A is singular this fails: A = [[1,0],[0,0]] sends both [[1,1],[1,1]] and [[1,1],[2,2]] to the same matrix [[1,1],[0,0]]. Matrices are not numbers.

For [[a,b],[c,d]] the determinant is ad − bc: multiply along the main diagonal, multiply along the other diagonal, then subtract. Adding the products (ad + bc) or stopping after one product are common slips.

Two checks. First, delete exactly row i and column j to form the minor Mij. Second, multiply by (−1)^(i+j): positions with i + j even keep the sign of the minor, positions with i + j odd flip it. For position (1, 2) the sign is −1, so a minor of −6 gives a cofactor of +6.

For an upper or lower triangular matrix the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries, not the sum, and the signs count: 2 · (−1) · 5 = −10. Entries off the diagonal play no role. (Cofactor expansion along the first column explains why.)

Track each operation: swapping two rows multiplies det by −1; multiplying one row by c multiplies det by c; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged. Apply them in order, starting from the original determinant, and do not count a replacement as a change.

The determinant is not additive: with A = B = I₂ you have det(A + B) = det(2I) = 4 but det A + det B = 2. For scaling, every one of the n rows is multiplied by c, so det(cA) = cⁿ det A. The rule that does hold for products is det(AB) = det A · det B.

List the facts you need and write each factor separately: det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, det(Aᵀ) = det A, det(A²) = (det A)², det(adj A) = (det A)ⁿ⁻¹ for an n × n matrix. Multiply the factors at the end and watch the signs, because det B can be negative.

When det A = 0 there is no unique solution, but a particular system Ax = b can still have solutions: it is inconsistent for some b and has infinitely many solutions for others. For A = [[1,2],[2,4]], Ax = (3, 6) has infinitely many solutions while Ax = (3, 7) has none.

Always test the pair: compute Av and compare with λv. For a given λ the eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of (A − λI)v = 0, so solve that system for the λ you were given, and check your vector in the original equation Av = λv.

The definition has two conditions: v ≠ 0 and Av = λv. Length one is a convenient normalisation, not a requirement; coordinates may be zero; and λ = 0 is a legitimate eigenvalue, which occurs precisely when A is singular. Do not add conditions that are not in the definition.

For a diagonal matrix, each standard basis vector ej is an eigenvector and its eigenvalue is the j-th diagonal entry, signs included. So diag(−2, 0, 5) has eigenvalues −2, 0 and 5 and nothing else. Read the diagonal, do not compute anything else.
Start from Av = λv and multiply by A⁻¹: v = λA⁻¹v, so A⁻¹v = (1/λ)v. The eigenvector stays the same and the eigenvalue becomes its reciprocal, sign included: for λ = −2 you get −1/2, not 1/2 or 4.

From AP = PD, column j of P is multiplied by dj, so dj must be the eigenvalue belonging to column j. Reordering the columns of P forces the same reordering of D. If you are unsure, test the first column: A·p1 must equal d1·p1.

Do not decide from the eigenvalues alone: count independent eigenvectors. A repeated eigenvalue can still give a full eigenvector basis (2I) or not ([[2,1],[0,2]]). For each eigenvalue solve (A − λI)v = 0 and see how many independent solutions you get; you need n in total.

Use Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ and pick out the entry by multiplying the right row of P, the diagonal Dᵏ and the right column of P⁻¹; then check the formula at k = 1, where you must get the original entry. For p(A)v = 0 look at the eigenvalues: when A has an eigenvector basis, exactly the eigenvectors whose eigenvalue is a root of p are sent to 0.

In ℝⁿ add component by component; for functions add pointwise, (f + g)(t) = f(t) + g(t). When you subtract, the minus sign applies to the whole of the second object: 2f − g subtracts every term of g. For linear combinations, a coefficient multiplies every coordinate of the vector it belongs to.

The zero vector 0 satisfies u + 0 = u for every u. In C(ℝ) addition is pointwise, so the zero vector must add nothing at every t: it is the function f(t) = 0. The constant function 1 is the identity for multiplication of functions, which is not an operation of the vector space.

Every linear map satisfies T(0) = T(0·0) = 0·T(0) = 0. So if T(0) ≠ 0, the map is not linear, as for a translation. The converse is false: T(x) = x² has T(0) = 0 but is not linear. To prove linearity check additivity and homogeneity for all vectors.

The j-th column of the standard matrix is T(ej). Compute T(1, 0) and T(0, 1) from the formula and write each result as a column. Then test the matrix: A·(x, y)ᵀ must reproduce the formula for T(x, y).

Test the two conditions with specific numbers. x + 1 fails because T(0) ≠ 0. x² fails additivity: (1 + 1)² = 4 but 1² + 1² = 2. |x| fails homogeneity: |−1 · 1| = 1 but −1 · |1| = −1. A map is linear only if both conditions hold for all vectors and scalars.

To find T⁻¹(w) solve T(v) = w, and then verify by applying T to your answer: you should get w back. In an eigenbasis, T acts as multiplication by λ on each eigenvector, so T⁻¹ divides by λ. For operators like (Sf)(t) = f(t) + f(0), evaluate at t = 0 first to find the unknown constant f(0).

The subspace test has three parts: contains 0, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiplication. A set can pass two and fail one. {(x, y): x ≥ 0} contains 0 and is closed under addition but fails scaling: −1 · (1, 0) = (−1, 0) leaves the set.

Re-read the definition in this topic and rework the question on paper, checking each step with a small example. Rating your confidence before the answer will tell you whether this was a slip or a gap.

The product rule turns a product inside the log into a sum of logs; it says nothing about a sum inside the log. Test it with numbers: ln(2 + 3) = ln 5 ≈ 1.609, but ln 2 + ln 3 ≈ 1.792. For ln(2e³) split the product first: ln 2 + ln(e³) = ln 2 + 3. The exponent 3 belongs to e only, so it multiplies ln e = 1, not ln 2.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses an inequality: −2x > −5 gives x < 5/2, not x > 5/2. Whenever you obtain a boundary, test one point from each side in the original condition (for ln(5 − 2x) try x = 0 and x = 3) before trusting the direction.

Read the domain and range off the formula. e^(−x) is strictly positive but never 0, so 3 + e^(−x) takes every value above 3 and never 3 itself. A shift moves the whole range. A restriction such as x ≤ 0 tells you which root to keep when you invert, and a log needs its argument strictly greater than 0.

σ turns a score z into a probability p. To go back you need the log-odds z = ln(p/(1 − p)), not p and not ln p. For p = 3/4 the odds are 3, so the score threshold is ln 3. For a model p = σ(b + wx) the log-odds are affine in x, so extrapolate those and convert back at the end.

If output goes from 60 to 96 in 3 years, the growth factor is 96/60 = 8/5 and e^(3k) = 8/5, not 3/5 (that is the increase). Then k = ln(8/5)/3 and doubling needs e^(kt) = 2, so t = ln 2 / k = 3 ln 2 / ln(8/5) ≈ 4.42 years. A quick sanity check: doubling takes more than the 3 years it took to grow by 60%.

For a composition, evaluate the outer derivative at the inner value and multiply by the inner derivative. For e^(3x−1) the inner function 3x − 1 has derivative 3, so the answer is 3e^(3x−1). Name the outer and inner functions and write one factor for each before you simplify; in a gradient the same applies, e.g. ∂(r²)/∂w = 2r · ∂r/∂w = 2r·x.

(ln x)′ = 1/x, the reciprocal. For ln(u(x)) you get u′(x)/u(x). Check it with numbers: ln grows slowly, so its slope at x = 10 should be small (0.1), not 10. For ln(5x) the factor 5 from the inner function cancels the 5 in the denominator: 5/(5x) = 1/x.

0/0 is not an answer; it is a signal to simplify. For x ≠ 3, (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = (x + 3)(x − 3)/(x − 3) = x + 3, whose limit at 3 is 6. A limit only looks at x near 3, never at x = 3, so cancelling the common factor is legitimate.

Keep the ladder straight: differentiable implies continuous, but not the reverse. |x| is continuous at 0 yet its difference quotient is −1 from the left and +1 from the right, so there is no derivative. At the join of two pieces you need equal values for continuity, equal slopes for differentiability, and equal second derivatives for a second derivative to exist.

A slope or derivative is a rate (output units per input unit). To obtain a change multiply by the size of the step: Δf ≈ f′(a)·Δx. To obtain an average rate over [a, b] divide the change by b − a. Decide which of these the question asks for, and check the units of your answer.

Power rule: (xᵖ)′ = p·xᵖ⁻¹; bring the exponent down and lower it by one. A constant multiple stays and the derivative of c·x is c. e^x is not a power of x: it is its own derivative (use the chain rule for an inner function). A product needs both terms: (fg)′ = f′g + fg′, not f′g′.

The second-order Taylor polynomial is f(a) + f′(a)h + ½f″(a)h², so the curvature term carries a ½ and the sign of f″. A centered difference cancels the quadratic term and is accurate to order h², while a forward or backward quotient has an error proportional to h. Write the approximation formula down before substituting numbers.

For ∂F/∂x₂ treat x₁ as a fixed number and differentiate each term as an ordinary function of x₂. In F = x₁²x₂ + 4x₂ both terms contain x₂, so ∂F/∂x₂ = x₁² + 4. Differentiate first and substitute the point afterwards; substituting x₁ = 0 first would wrongly turn x₁ into a constant.

A rate per unit distance needs a unit vector, so divide v by ‖v‖ first (‖(3, −4)‖ = 5). Then take the dot product ∇F · u, keeping every sign. Along the steepest direction g/‖g‖ the rate is ‖g‖, not ‖g‖².

∇F · u = ‖∇F‖ cos α is largest when u points along the gradient, so ∇F points uphill. The steepest decrease is in direction −∇F/‖∇F‖ and its rate is −‖∇F‖. A direction perpendicular to ∇F has first-order change 0, which is neither an increase nor a decrease.

Write the conventions down first: rᵢ = ŷᵢ − yᵢ, MSE = (1/m)Σrᵢ², half-MSE = (1/2m)Σrᵢ², and ∇MSE = 2·∇half-MSE. A positive residual means overprediction. Then differentiate with the chain rule, e.g. for sigmoid loss ∇ℓ = (p − y)·p(1 − p)·a, where the sign comes from p − y.

Existing partial derivatives say something only about slices along the axes. For F = st²/(s² + t²) (with F(0, 0) = 0) both partials at the origin are 0, yet along u = (3/5, 4/5) the rate is 48/125 ≠ 0. Differentiability needs one linear approximation that works for every direction; it is guaranteed when the partials exist nearby and are continuous.

∇L = 0 is a system with one equation per parameter. For ŷ = b + wx under half-MSE it is Σrᵢ = 0 (intercept) AND Σrᵢxᵢ = 0 (slope). A residual vector can satisfy the first and still fail the second, so check both.

The minus sign belongs in the update: x_new = x_old − η·g. Where a gradient component is negative the loss falls as that coordinate increases, so subtracting a negative number moves you to the right. If the loss went up after one step, check the sign before you blame the learning rate.

At an interior local minimiser of a differentiable function ∇L = 0 — a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Stationary points can be minima, maxima or neither: x², −x² and x³ all have derivative 0 at 0. The minimum value need not be 0 either: L = 4 + (x − 3)² has minimum value 4 at x = 3.

A global minimum on a closed interval means comparing L at every candidate: the stationary points and the endpoints. For L = x³ − 3x on [−2, 3] the candidates −2, −1, 1, 3 give −2, 2, −2, 18. In least squares the minimiser is unique only if the design-matrix columns are independent; with repeated x values a whole line of parameter pairs is optimal.

The update is η·∇L, so doubling the loss doubles the step: with MSE instead of half-MSE you need half the learning rate to get identical iterates. For L = (x − 2)² the error is multiplied by 1 − 2η at each step and shrinks only if |1 − 2η| < 1. With several curvatures the steepest one limits η (η < 2/λmax), and the best fixed rate balances the extremes.

Step length = η·‖g‖, so with η = 10⁻⁶ and ‖g‖ = 20 the step is 2 × 10⁻⁵, below the threshold, while the gradient 20 is nowhere near 0. A tiny step may only mean a tiny learning rate. Test ‖g‖ ≤ ε for stationarity; use step and loss changes only as extra signs of stalled progress.

Before choosing an answer to a calculus question, say what is being asked for (a value, a rate, a change, a direction or a minimiser), write the rule you will use, and then check your result with a quick number test. Many wrong answers here come from a missing factor or a flipped sign, and a quick numerical check usually exposes them.

An event is a set of outcomes from the sample space, so it has to be built from outcomes such as HT and TH, not from numerical values like 0, 1 or 2. The count of heads is a function of the outcome (a random variable). To write an event, ask which outcomes make the statement true and list exactly those.

The outcomes in A ∩ B are counted once inside P(A) and again inside P(B). Subtract the overlap once: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Plain addition is correct only when A and B are disjoint. A quick check: a union can never have probability larger than 1.

Conditioning on B shrinks the sample space to B, so you must divide the shared probability P(A ∩ B) by P(B). Leaving out the division gives a joint probability, and multiplying instead of dividing gives something that is not a probability of A given B at all. Write P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) first, then substitute.

Independence is about probabilities (P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)); disjointness is about outcomes (A ∩ B is empty). If A and B are disjoint and both have positive probability, then P(A ∩ B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0, so they cannot be independent. Knowing that one of them occurred tells you the other did not, which is the opposite of 'no information'.

P(positive | disease) and P(disease | positive) answer different questions: the first conditions on the sick people, the second on everyone who tested positive. They are linked by Bayes' rule, which brings in the base rate P(disease). With a rare condition, most positives come from the large healthy group, so P(disease | positive) is much smaller than the sensitivity.

The law of total probability is a weighted sum over the entire partition: P(A) = Σ P(A | Bi)P(Bi). Each conditional probability must be multiplied by the probability of its branch, and every branch must be included. A plain average treats the branches as equally likely, and a single branch ignores the others. The same weighting is used for total expectation.

Read the event carefully: P(Aᶜ ∩ B) is the part of B where A does not happen, so it equals P(B) − P(A ∩ B). With independence, that is P(Aᶜ)P(B). Reporting P(A ∩ B) or P(Aᶜ) alone answers a different question. Drawing a two-circle diagram and shading the target region prevents this slip.

Two flags that are independent given the state contribute the product of their likelihoods: 0.9² under disease and 0.1² under no disease. Using one flag gives the single-flag posterior, which is too small here. Put both likelihoods into the numerator and the total-probability denominator, then apply Bayes' rule once.

A random variable is a function X that assigns one real number to each outcome. It is not a probability, the numbers need not be equally likely (a head count of 1 is twice as likely as 0 for two fair coins), and different outcomes can map to the same number (HT and TH both give 1). Probabilities come from the model, and a random variable only attaches numbers to outcomes.

For a continuous variable, probabilities are areas under the density, so P(X = x0) = 0 for every single x0. The height f(x0) is a density per unit length and can be larger than 1 on a short interval (Uniform(0, 0.5) has height 2) as long as the total area is 1. Use an integral over an interval, or the CDF, to get a probability.

Standardize with Z = (X − μ) / σ: subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation σ, which is the square root of the variance. For N(10, 4) the standard deviation is 2, not 4. Then remember that Φ(z) is a cumulative probability P(Z ≤ z), so an interval needs Φ(upper) − Φ(lower), and 'within two standard deviations' of the mean is a different, two-sided interval.

For exactly k successes in n independent trials, count the arrangements C(n, k), then multiply by p to the power k for the successes and (1 − p) to the power n − k for the failures. Swapping the exponents computes the probability of n − k successes, changing k changes the answer, and p alone is just the success probability of one trial.

Start from the CDF: F_U(u) = P(g(X) ≤ u), rewrite the event in terms of X, then differentiate. A decreasing map such as U = 2 − 3X turns U ≤ u into X ≥ (2 − u)/3, so you use 1 − F_X, and differentiating brings in the factor 1/3 from the chain rule. Finally check that the new density integrates to 1 on the new support.

For X ~ Uniform(a, b), probability is interval length divided by the support length b − a, and the variance is (b − a)²/12. The factor 12 comes from integrating (x − mean)² against a flat density. Write both formulas down and substitute a = 2, b = 8 carefully.

For a 0/1 variable, X² = X, so E(X²) = p and V(X) = p − p² = p(1 − p). The variance is not p (that is the mean) and not p² (that is the square of the mean). A quick check at p = 1/4: the variance is (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16, and it is largest at p = 1/2.

E(X²) is the second raw moment, not the variance. The variance measures spread around the mean: V(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Compute the mean first, square it, and subtract it from E(X²). For f(x) = 2x on (0, 1): E(X²) = 1/2 and E(X) = 2/3, so V(X) = 1/2 − 4/9 = 1/18.

Variance is not linear. A shift b moves every value by the same amount, so it does not change spread, and a scale a multiplies every deviation by a, so the squared deviations are multiplied by a². Hence V(aX + b) = a²V(X) and the standard deviation scales by |a|. Multiplying measurements by ten multiplies the variance by one hundred.

Look up what the parameter means before using it. For Poisson(λ) the mean and variance are both λ. For the exponential in this course β is the scale, which is also the mean, and the variance is β². The reciprocal 1/β is the rate, and it is not the mean. Using the wrong convention changes the numbers by exactly these factors.

E[(X − c)²] is the mean squared distance from c, not from the mean. Expanding around the mean gives V(X) + [E(X) − c]². If c equals the mean, only the variance remains; otherwise the squared offset is added. This is the same bias-variance split you will meet again in the mean square error of an estimator.

Expectation is linear without any independence assumption: E(aX + bY + c) = aE(X) + bE(Y) + c whenever the means exist. Independence matters for the variance of a sum, where V(X + Y) = V(X) + V(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y), and for identifying a distribution such as the binomial. That is why E(K) = np holds even for dependent trials with the same p.

The marginal mass function of X is p_X(x) = Σ_y p_{X,Y}(x, y): hold x fixed and add up the joint probabilities over all y, which in a table means summing the column for that x. Summing over x gives the marginal of Y, and dividing by or multiplying with p_Y changes it into something else (a conditional, or a product).

The implication goes one way only: independent ⇒ Cov(X, Y) = 0. Covariance measures linear association, so a perfectly dependent pair such as X and X² (for X symmetric about 0) can have covariance 0. To show independence you must check that the joint distribution factorizes for every pair of values, not just that the covariance vanishes.

E(X | Y = y) is the average of X under the conditional distribution given Y = y, so it is a number measured in the units of X (not a probability, and not a mean of Y). If the conditioning value is left random, E(X | Y) becomes a random variable, a function of Y. For a 0/1 variable the conditional mean equals the conditional probability P(X = 1 | Y = y).

A conditional distribution of X given Y = y is the joint divided by the marginal of Y: p(x | y) = p(x, y)/p_Y(y), or f(x | y) = f(x, y)/f_Y(y) for densities. A joint entry like 0.15 is the probability of both events, and a marginal like 0.20 ignores Y. Neither sums to 1 over x for the fixed y. In the continuous case divide by the marginal density f_Y(y), not by a point probability, which is 0.

Variance of a sum needs the covariance: V(aX + bY) = a²V(X) + b²V(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y). The middle term carries the product ab, so it changes sign when one coefficient is negative, as in 2X − Y. Only for independent (or uncorrelated) variables does the covariance term vanish.

A correlation or a dependence in a joint table says the variables move together, not that one produces the other. Device type might be linked to the action through the kind of visitor, the page, or the time of day. Causal claims need a design that controls those factors, such as a randomized experiment.

σ describes the spread of individual observations; the standard error σ/√n describes the spread of the sample mean across repeated samples, and it is smaller because averaging cancels some of the noise. With σ = 12 and n = 36 the standard error is 12/6 = 2, not 12.

The standard error is σ/√n, so it shrinks like the square root of n, not like n. Quadrupling the sample size halves it; to halve the error you need four times as much data. Calculate the square root of n first, and only then divide σ by it.

Parameters such as μ, σ² and p are fixed numbers, even if we do not know them. A statistic such as the sample mean is computed from the sample, so it changes from one sample to the next. The randomness in an estimate comes from the sampling, which is why we describe it with a sampling distribution.

The law of large numbers says X̄ converges to μ (the sample mean concentrates). The central limit theorem says the standardized error √n(X̄ − μ)/σ has a distribution that approaches N(0, 1), so probabilities about X̄ can be approximated. It does not change the distribution of the individual observations, and for a non-normal population X̄ is only approximately normal and the quality of the approximation depends on n and the population shape.

The values x1, …, xn in one sample are one realization of the data and their histogram estimates the population distribution. The sampling distribution is something else: the distribution of a statistic such as X̄ over all the samples you could have drawn. Imagine repeating the whole sampling process many times and recording X̄ each time.

The unbiased sample variance divides the sum of squared deviations from X̄ by n − 1, because deviations from the sample mean are smaller than deviations from the true mean. The MLE of the normal variance divides by n and its expectation is (n − 1)/n × σ², so it is biased downward. Check which estimator the question asks for, and then divide the centred sum of squares by the right number.

Unbiased means E(θ̂) = θ: the centre of the sampling distribution is on target. Any single estimate can still be far from θ, and the spread of the sampling distribution (its variance) can be large. How far an estimator typically misses combines both bias and spread in the mean squared error: MSE = V + bias².

The parameter is a fixed number; the interval is what changes from sample to sample. The 95% is the long-run fraction of intervals produced by the procedure that contain the parameter. After the data are in, a particular interval either contains the parameter or it does not. It is not a range for individual observations, and it does not promise that exactly 95 of 100 intervals cover (only that about 95% do on average).

A confidence interval is estimate ± critical value × standard error. The critical value is 1.96 for a normal-based 95% interval, but when σ is estimated by s from a normal sample you use the t quantile with n − 1 degrees of freedom (2.131 for n = 16), which is larger because it accounts for estimating the spread. Leaving the critical value out gives an interval that is far too narrow.

The mean squared error of an estimator is V(θ̂) + [B(θ̂)]². If the estimator is biased, the variance alone understates the typical squared error. Compute the bias E(θ̂) − θ first, square it, and add it to the variance. A biased estimator can still have a smaller MSE than an unbiased one when its variance is much smaller.

For two unbiased estimators the efficiency of θ̂1 relative to θ̂2 is V(θ̂2)/V(θ̂1); a value above 1 means θ̂1 is more precise (smaller variance). When you combine independent unbiased estimators, the weights should be proportional to 1/variance, so the more precise estimator receives the larger weight: w = V2/(V1 + V2) for T1.

The method of moments matches a population moment, written in terms of the parameter, to the sample moment: for Uniform(0, θ), θ/2 = x̄ so θ̂ = 2x̄. Maximum likelihood instead maximizes the likelihood of the observed data: for 8 successes and 12 failures the log-likelihood is 8 log p + 12 log(1 − p), whose maximum is at 8/20. The two methods agree for the Bernoulli but not in general (for Uniform(0, θ) the MLE is the sample maximum).

Re-read the question and say in one sentence what is given, what is being asked, and what is conditioned on. Then redo the calculation with a small concrete case, such as 10,000 people, a short table, or a simple distribution, and compare it with your answer. If the two disagree, the explanation under the question shows where the reasoning diverges.
The variance along an eigenvector of the covariance matrix **equals its eigenvalue**, so the largest eigenvalue marks the direction of greatest spread. Recompute both eigenvalues and compare.
The off-diagonal entry is the covariance between the variables and tilts the principal axis away from the coordinate axes. Always find eigenvectors; do not read the answer off the diagonal.
The gradient points uphill (direction of steepest **increase**). To reduce the loss move the opposite way: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\nabla L$.
Take each partial derivative separately, treating the other variable as a constant: $\partial/\partial w_2\,(3w_2^2)=6w_2$.
Read the question for the quantity being asked: $\sigma(0)=0.5$ but the slope is $\sigma(0)(1-\sigma(0))=0.25$.

The posterior divides by the **total** probability of the evidence: $P(\text{spam}\mid\text{word})=P(\text{word}\mid\text{spam})P(\text{spam})/P(\text{word})$, with $P(\text{word})$ from the law of total probability.
$P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$ are different numbers; Bayes' rule is exactly the bridge between them, and it needs the prior.
$\mu$ is fixed and the interval is already computed, so it either contains $\mu$ or not. The $95\%$ is the long-run proportion of intervals built this way that capture $\mu$.
The mean of $n$ observations varies less than a single observation: its standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt n$. A confidence interval for $\mu$ must use that.
Covariance measures only **linear** association. $Y=X^2$ with $X$ symmetric about $0$ has zero covariance but is fully dependent on $X$.

lessons.title: Course overview and syllabus
lessons.description: Aim, ten learning outcomes, the three parts, the 15 topics and how you are assessed.
objectives: Name the three parts of the course and the topics each contains
Relate each learning outcome (LO.1–LO.10) to the kind of task you will be asked to do
Plan your 45 hours: 15 hours in class and 30 hours of independent practice
lessons.body:
Machine learning is applied mathematics. A model is a function with parameters, training is optimisation of those parameters, and the data it learns from is uncertain. This course gives you exactly the three mathematical languages behind that sentence — **linear algebra** for representing data and transformations, **calculus** for measuring change and optimising, and **probability and statistics** for reasoning under uncertainty.

> [!ghi-nho] The emphasis is on **mathematical reasoning and interpretation in data science and machine learning contexts**, not on memorising formulas. When you finish a topic you should be able to say what an object *means* (a matrix as a transformation, a gradient as the direction of steepest increase, a confidence interval as a statement about a procedure) and when to use it.

## Course facts

| | |
|---|---|
| Class contact | 15 hours |
| Independent study | 30 hours |
| Total workload | 45 hours |
| Structure | 3 parts · 15 topics |

## The three parts

| Part | Module | Class hours | Topics |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Linear Algebra | 5 | 1 Linear systems · 2 Matrix operations and inverses · 3 Determinants · 4 Eigenvalues and eigenvectors · 5 Vector spaces and linear mappings |
| II | Calculus and Optimization for Machine Learning | 5 | 6 Functions, exponentials and logarithms · 7 Derivatives, chain rule and marginal effects · 8 Partial derivatives and the gradient · 9 Optimization and gradient descent |
| III | Introduction to Probability and Statistics | 5 | 10 Probability foundations · 11 Random variables and distributions · 12 Expectation, variance and moments · 13 Joint distributions and dependence · 14 Sampling distributions and the CLT · 15 Estimation and confidence intervals |

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the course you can:

- **LO.1 (Understand)** Explain the concepts and terminology of linear algebra, calculus and optimization, and probability and statistics.
- **LO.2 (Understand)** Explain the structure and solution of linear systems and the main properties and operations of matrices.
- **LO.3 (Understand)** Explain determinants, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, vector spaces and linear mappings.
- **LO.4 (Understand)** Explain functions, limits, derivatives, the chain rule, marginal effects, partial derivatives and gradients.
- **LO.5 (Apply)** Apply derivatives and gradients to analyse functions and basic optimization problems, including gradient descent.
- **LO.6 (Apply)** Apply probability rules, conditional probability, independence, the law of total probability and Bayes' rule.
- **LO.7 (Apply)** Work with random variables, mass and density functions, cumulative distributions, common distributions, expectation and variance.
- **LO.8 (Analyze)** Analyse joint, marginal and conditional distributions, dependence, covariance, correlation and conditional expectation.
- **LO.9 (Analyze)** Analyse sampling distributions and estimators using bias, variance, mean square error, confidence intervals, efficiency and consistency.
- **LO.10 (Evaluate)** Select and justify the mathematical concepts and procedures that suit a structured data science or machine learning problem.

## How you are assessed

| Component | Weight | What it looks like | LOs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quiz / short analytical test | 20% | Short-answer and problem-based questions on definitions, calculations and interpretation | LO.1–LO.7 |
| Problem-solving assignment | 30% | Structured problems from all three parts, with your reasoning explained | LO.2–LO.9 |
| Integrated final assessment | 50% | Scenarios where you choose and apply methods from the whole course | LO.2–LO.10 |

The quizzes in this course follow the first component: every wrong answer is linked to a specific misconception, and the feedback tells you *where the reasoning went wrong*, not just that it did.

## How to study each topic

1. Read the lesson and **try each worked example yourself before opening the next step**.
2. Do the topic quiz. Rate your confidence before you see the answer — knowing that you are unsure is information.
3. Review the flashcards the next day, then a week later.
4. Read the lecture notes PDF for the full derivations and look at the slides before class.

## Recommended resources

The lecture notes and slides attached to each part are the primary text. For further reading, see the textbooks listed in the syllabus (Strang, *Introduction to Linear Algebra*; Boyd & Vandenberghe, *Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra*; Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning*; Wasserman, *All of Statistics*).
summary: The course has three parts and fifteen topics; each part is five class hours.
Quizzes (20%), the problem-solving assignment (30%) and the integrated final assessment (50%) together test LO.1–LO.10.
Study by attempting every step yourself first, using the quiz confidence rating, and reviewing flashcards on a spaced schedule.

lessons.body:
Part I comes with two PDFs written by the course team. They use the same notation as the lessons, so you can move between them freely.

- **Lecture notes (17 pages).** Definitions, theorems and worked examples with short proofs and checks. Use them for the full derivations.
- **Lecture slides (51 slides).** The same content as a compact outline with one worked example per idea. Use them to preview a topic or to revise quickly.

## Where each topic is

| Topic | Lecture notes | Slides |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Linear systems | pp. 2–4 | 4–11 |
| 2 Matrix operations and inverse matrices | pp. 5–8 | 13–26 |
| 3 Determinants | pp. 9–11 | 28–34 |
| 4 Eigenvalues and eigenvectors (including diagonalization) | pp. 12–15 | 35–43 |
| 5 Vector spaces and linear mappings | pp. 16–17 | 45–51 |

## How to use them

1. **Before a topic:** skim the slides to see the shape of the topic.
2. **In the lesson:** try every worked example yourself before you reveal the next step, then do the topic quiz with a confidence rating for each question.
3. **After the quiz:** read the matching pages of the lecture notes. They contain derivations that the lessons only summarise, such as why $AP=PD$ gives a diagonalization.
4. **For revision:** use the flashcards at the end of each lesson, then return to the slides.

> [!meo] All scalars are real numbers unless stated otherwise. Row operations are written $R_i \leftarrow R_i + cR_j$, and $A^\top$ denotes the transpose, in the lessons as in the PDFs.

lessons.title: Topic 1 · Linear Systems
lessons.description: Linear equations, augmented matrices, elementary row operations, Gaussian elimination and Gauss–Jordan, and how to read no / one / infinitely many solutions from the echelon form.
objectives: Decide whether an equation is linear and write a linear system as an augmented matrix and as Ax = b
Apply the three elementary row operations correctly and explain why each preserves the solution set
Reduce an augmented matrix to row echelon form and solve by back-substitution or Gauss–Jordan elimination
Classify a system as having no, one or infinitely many solutions from its echelon form
Write the general solution of a consistent system with free variables as a particular solution plus homogeneous solutions
Explain why a homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations has nonzero solutions
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
Almost every data-science method asks you, sooner or later, to solve a system of linear equations. Fitting a line to data by least squares, balancing the flows in a network, or finding the weights of a small model all come down to finding numbers that satisfy several linear conditions at once. This lesson gives you the one algorithm that does it reliably, **Gaussian elimination**, and the language (matrices, pivots, free variables) for reading the answer.

> [!ghi-nho] A linear system has **no solution**, **exactly one** solution, or **infinitely many**. Never exactly two. Elimination tells you which case you are in.

:::Predict before you read
A system has $2$ equations and $3$ unknowns. Can it have **exactly one** solution? Write down yes or no and a one-line reason. You will check your prediction at the end of the free-variables example.
:::

sections.title: Linear equations and linear systems

parts.title: Linear
parts.md:
- $3x - 2y = 5$
- $2x_1 - 3x_2 = 5$
- $x_1 + 0\,x_2 - x_3 = 4$ (a zero coefficient is allowed)
- $4x = 12$

parts.title: Not linear
parts.md:
- $x_1x_2 = 5$ (product of unknowns)
- $x^2 + y = 1$ (a power)
- $e^{x} + y = 0$ (a function of an unknown)
- $\sin x_1 = 0$

sections.intro: A **linear equation** in $n$ unknowns has the form $a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 + \dots + a_nx_n = b$, where the coefficients $a_i$ and the right-hand side $b$ are fixed real numbers. A **linear system** is a collection of $m$ such equations in the same $n$ unknowns. A **solution** is one vector $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ that satisfies **every** equation at the same time. Two systems are **equivalent** when they have exactly the same solution set.
sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] Each term must be a fixed number times a single unknown. Products of unknowns, powers, and functions such as $\sin x$ or $e^x$ make an equation nonlinear, however simple it looks.

sections.title: Three ways to write one system

parts.title: Equations
parts.md:
$$\begin{cases} 2x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 8 \\ -3x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = -11 \\ -2x_1 + x_2 + 2x_3 = -3 \end{cases}$$

Three equations in the three unknowns $x_1, x_2, x_3$.

parts.title: Augmented matrix
parts.md:
The **coefficient matrix** $A$ stores only the coefficients; appending the right-hand side gives $[A \mid b]$.

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix},\qquad [A\mid b]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 & -11 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -3\end{array}\right]$$

The column order must match the order of the unknowns.

parts.title: Matrix equation
parts.md:
$$\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8 \\ -11 \\ -3\end{pmatrix}\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Ax=b$$

Here $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $x$ is the column of unknowns and $b$ the column of right-hand sides.

sections.intro: One system, three notations. You will move between them all the time.
sections.outro:
**Is $(2, 3, -1)$ a solution?** Substitute into every equation: $2(2)+3-(-1)=8$, $-3(2)-3+2(-1)=-11$ and $-2(2)+3+2(-1)=-3$. All three hold, so yes.

> [!canh-bao] Checking only the first equation proves nothing. A vector is a solution only if it satisfies all equations of the system.

sections.title: The three elementary row operations

parts.title: Interchange
parts.md:
$R_i \leftrightarrow R_j$

Swap two rows. This only lists the equations in a different order.

parts.title: Scaling
parts.md:
$R_i \leftarrow cR_i \quad (c \neq 0)$

Multiply every entry of a row by a **nonzero** number. This multiplies an equation by a constant.

parts.title: Replacement
parts.md:
$R_i \leftarrow R_i + cR_j$

Add a multiple of one row to another row. This is adding (or subtracting) equations, the move you know from algebra.

sections.intro: These three operations change the matrix but never change the solution set.
sections.outro:
**Why they are safe:** each can be undone (swap again; scale by $1/c$; subtract $cR_j$ again), so no information is lost and the new system is equivalent to the old one.

> [!canh-bao] Multiplying a row by $0$ is **not** allowed, and neither is replacing a row by a copy of another row: both destroy an equation. A row operation also changes the **whole** row, the entry after the bar included.

sections.title: Worked example: Gaussian elimination

parts.title: Write the augmented matrix
