[[-0.8165 -0.8165 -0.8165]
 [-0.4082  0.4082  0.4082]
 [ 0.4082 -0.4082  0.4082]]
True
True
True
``` Exact diagonalization with `sympy`. The columns of `P` may be ordered or scaled differently from ours, but `P * D * P**-1` is always `B`. ```html 
import sympy as sp

B = sp.Matrix([[2, 0, 0], [0, 3, 4], [0, 4, 9]])
P, D = B.diagonalize()            # B = P D P^{-1}
print("P =", P)
print("D =", D)
print("P D P^-1 == B:", P * D * P.inv() == B)

# powers: compare (B^n)[1, 1] with (4 + 11^n)/5
print("(B^n)[1,1]:", [(B**n)[1, 1] for n in (1, 2, 3)])
print("(4 + 11^n)/5:", [sp.Rational(4 + 11**n, 5) for n in (1, 2, 3)])
``` **Output** ```html 
P = Matrix([[0, 1, 0], [-2, 0, 1], [1, 0, 2]])
D = Matrix([[1, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, 0, 11]])
P D P^-1 == B: True
(B^n)[1,1]: [3, 25, 267]
(4 + 11^n)/5: [3, 25, 267]
```

items.meaning: A nonzero v with Av = λv. Nothing else is required: λ may be 0 and v may have zero entries and any length.
det(A − λI) = 0. Its roots are the eigenvalues; for each, solve (A − λI)v = 0 for the eigenvectors.
The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
Sum of eigenvalues = trace; product of eigenvalues = det A. Use them as a check.
If Av = λv then Aᵏv = λᵏv, p(A)v = p(λ)v and, for invertible A, A⁻¹v = λ⁻¹v.
A = PDP⁻¹ with P invertible and D diagonal. Equivalent: A has n linearly independent eigenvectors.
Columns of P are eigenvectors; D has the matching eigenvalues in the same order (AP = PD).
items.note: Column order and eigenvalue order must agree.

items.meaning: Repeated eigenvalues may give too few eigenvectors. [[2, 1], [0, 2]] has one eigenvector line and is not diagonalizable; 2I is.
Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ with Dᵏ = diag(λ₁ᵏ, …, λₙᵏ).

summary: An eigenvector v ≠ 0 of A satisfies Av = λv: A only stretches it by the eigenvalue λ.
Eigenvalues are the roots of det(A − λI) = 0; eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of (A − λI)v = 0. Always check Av = λv.
Diagonal and triangular matrices have their diagonal entries as eigenvalues; eigenvalues add to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
A is diagonalizable exactly when it has n independent eigenvectors; then A = PDP⁻¹ with D in the same order as the columns of P.
Powers and polynomials of A act on eigenvectors by powers and polynomials of λ, so Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $v = (-2, 1, 1)^\top$, which value satisfies $Av = \lambda v$?
questions.explanation: Multiplying gives $Av=(1\cdot(-2)+2\cdot1-2\cdot1,\ 1\cdot(-2)+2\cdot1+1\cdot1,\ (-1)(-2)+(-1)(1)+0)=(-2,1,1)^\top=1\cdot v$. Since $v\neq0$, the eigenvalue is $1$. The other numbers give a different vector. (Note that $3$ and $-1$ are eigenvalues of $A$, but with other eigenvectors.)

questions.prompt: Which condition is part of the definition of an eigenvector $v$?
questions.explanation: An eigenvector must be nonzero, because $A\cdot 0=\lambda\cdot 0$ holds for every $\lambda$ and would make the idea meaningless. Nothing else is required: coordinates may be zero, any length is allowed, and the eigenvalue may be $0$ (exactly when $A$ is singular).

questions.prompt: What is the set of eigenvalues of $D = \operatorname{diag}(-2, 0, 5)$?
questions.explanation: For a diagonal matrix each standard basis vector $e_j$ is an eigenvector, and its eigenvalue is the $j$-th diagonal entry. So the eigenvalues are $-2$, $0$ and $5$, with their signs.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is invertible and $Av = -2v$ with $v \neq 0$, which statement holds?
questions.explanation: Multiply $Av=-2v$ by $A^{-1}$ to get $v=-2A^{-1}v$, and divide by $-2$: $A^{-1}v=-\tfrac12 v$. Inversion replaces a nonzero eigenvalue by its reciprocal and keeps the eigenvector.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, which gives all eigenvectors for $\lambda = -1$, with $t \neq 0$?
questions.explanation: Solve $(A+I)v=0$. The rows give $x+y-z=0$ and $x+3y+z=0$ (the third row repeats the first). Subtracting gives $2y+2z=0$, so $y=-z$ and then $x=z-y=2z$. Every eigenvector is $t(2,-1,1)^\top$. Check: $A(2,-1,1)^\top=(-2,1,-1)^\top=-1\cdot(2,-1,1)^\top$. Option B is an eigenvector for $\lambda=1$ and option D for $\lambda=3$.

questions.prompt: For $B = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 9\end{pmatrix}$, choose $P = [(0,-2,1)^\top\ (1,0,0)^\top\ (0,1,2)^\top]$. Which $D$ satisfies $B = PDP^{-1}$?
questions.explanation: Compute $B$ times each column: $B(0,-2,1)^\top=(0,-2,1)^\top$ (eigenvalue $1$), $B(1,0,0)^\top=2\cdot(1,0,0)^\top$ (eigenvalue $2$) and $B(0,1,2)^\top=(0,11,22)^\top=11\cdot(0,1,2)^\top$ (eigenvalue $11$). So $BP=P\operatorname{diag}(1,2,11)$, and $P$ is invertible because its columns are independent ($\det P=5$). The diagonal order must match the column order.

questions.prompt: For which real $t$ is $A_t = \begin{pmatrix}2 & t & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$?
questions.explanation: If $t=0$ the matrix is already diagonal. If $t\neq0$, solving $(A_t-2I)v=0$ forces $y=0$ and $z=0$, so the eigenvalue $2$ has only one independent eigenvector $(1,0,0)^\top$; the eigenvalue $3$ contributes only $e_3$. That is two independent eigenvectors for a $3\times3$ matrix, so there is no eigenvector basis and no diagonalization.

questions.prompt: Let $B = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & 9\end{pmatrix}$. For every positive integer $k$, what is $(B^k)_{23}$?
questions.explanation: Use $B^k=P\operatorname{diag}(1,2^k,11^k)P^{-1}$. Row 2 of $P$ is $(-2,0,1)$ and column 3 of $P^{-1}$ is $(\tfrac15,0,\tfrac25)^\top$, so $(B^k)_{23}=(-2)(1)(\tfrac15)+0+(1)(11^k)(\tfrac25)=\dfrac{2(11^k-1)}{5}$. Check at $k=1$: $\frac{2\cdot10}{5}=4$, the original entry $B_{23}$. At $k=2$ it gives $48$, which matches $(B^2)_{23}$.

questions.prompt: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, which is the complete solution set of $(A^2 - I_3)x = 0$, with $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$?
questions.explanation: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1,-1,3$ with an eigenvector basis, and $(A^2-I)v=(\lambda^2-1)v$ for an eigenvector. The polynomial $\lambda^2-1$ vanishes at $1$ and $-1$ but not at $3$, so the kernel is spanned by $(-2,1,1)^\top$ and $(2,-1,1)^\top$, which is the plane $x_1=-2x_2$ with $x_3$ free. Directly: $A^2-I$ has rows $(4,8,0)$, $(2,4,0)$, $(-2,-4,0)$, i.e. the single condition $x_1+2x_2=0$.

questions.prompt: Find the **larger** eigenvalue of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: $\det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)(-2-\lambda)-4=\lambda^2+\lambda-6=(\lambda+3)(\lambda-2)$, so the eigenvalues are $-3$ and $2$. The larger one is $2$. (Check: trace $-1=-3+2$ and determinant $-6=(-3)(2)$.)

questions.prompt: A matrix with a repeated eigenvalue is never diagonalizable.
questions.explanation: False. $2I_2$ has the repeated eigenvalue $2$ and is already diagonal. Diagonalizability depends on whether there are $n$ independent eigenvectors, not on whether the eigenvalues repeat. ($\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ is a repeated-eigenvalue matrix that is not diagonalizable.)

questions.prompt: If $0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, then $A$ is invertible.
questions.explanation: False. $Av=0\cdot v=0$ with $v\neq 0$ means $A$ sends a nonzero vector to $0$, so $A$ is singular. A square matrix is invertible exactly when $0$ is **not** an eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for diagonalizing an $n\times n$ matrix in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Eigenvalues first; then eigenvectors for each; check that there are $n$ independent ones (otherwise stop: not diagonalizable); then assemble $P$ and $D$ in the same order; finally verify $AP=PD$.
sequence: Solve det(A − λI) = 0 for the eigenvalues
For each eigenvalue solve (A − λI)v = 0
Check that you have n linearly independent eigenvectors
Put the eigenvectors in the columns of P and the eigenvalues in the same order on the diagonal of D
Verify AP = PD

questions.prompt: $Av=3v$ with $v\neq 0$. Then $(A^2+2A+I)v=\mu v$. Enter $\mu$.
questions.explanation: $A^2v=3^2v=9v$ and $2Av=6v$, so $(A^2+2A+I)v=(9+6+1)v=16v$. In general $p(A)v=p(\lambda)v$ with $p(\lambda)=\lambda^2+2\lambda+1=(\lambda+1)^2=16$.

lessons.title: Topic 5 · Vector Spaces and Linear Mappings
lessons.description: Vector-space axioms, the main examples (Rⁿ, matrices, functions), subspaces, linear mappings, standard matrices, affine maps, and inverses of linear maps.
objectives: State the vector-space axioms and decide which one fails for a proposed set with its operations
Compute sums, scalar multiples and zero vectors in Rⁿ, in spaces of matrices and in C(ℝ)
Apply the subspace test and explain which of its three conditions a set fails
Test whether a map is linear using additivity, homogeneity and the quick test T(0) = 0
Construct the standard matrix of a linear map from a formula or from its values on a basis, and evaluate T from it
Distinguish linear from affine maps, compose maps, and find the inverse of a linear map via its matrix
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
Linear algebra is not only about columns of numbers. Matrices and functions can be added and scaled in exactly the same way, so the same ideas apply to them: they are all **vectors** in a **vector space**. A **linear map** is a function between vector spaces that respects addition and scaling, and in $\mathbb{R}^n$ every such map is a matrix. That is how data science sees a model: each layer of a neural network is a linear map plus a shift followed by a nonlinearity, and PCA is a projection, itself a linear map.

> [!ghi-nho] A map $T$ is linear if taking a linear combination before applying $T$ gives the same result as taking it afterwards: $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$.

:::Predict before you read
Is $T(x,y)=(x+1,\ y)$ linear? It looks very simple. Compute $T(0,0)$ and decide, then check your reasoning in the worked example on linear maps.
:::

sections.title: The ten axioms in four groups

parts.title: Addition
parts.md: For $u,v,w\in V$: closure $u+v\in V$; commutativity $u+v=v+u$; associativity $u+(v+w)=(u+v)+w$.

parts.title: Zero and negatives
parts.md: There is a **zero vector** $0_V$ with $u+0_V=u$ for every $u$; every $u$ has a negative $-u$ with $u+(-u)=0_V$.

parts.title: Scaling
parts.md: For scalars $c,d\in\mathbb{R}$: closure $cu\in V$; $c(du)=(cd)u$; and $1u=u$.

parts.title: Distributive laws
parts.md: $c(u+v)=cu+cv$ and $(c+d)u=cu+du$.

sections.intro: A **real vector space** is a nonempty set $V$ with addition of vectors and multiplication by real scalars that obey ten rules. A 'vector' is then any element of such a set: an arrow, a column of numbers, a matrix, a function.
sections.outro: These rules imply $0u=0_V$, $c\,0_V=0_V$ and $(-1)u=-u$. To show that something is **not** a vector space, find one rule that fails.

sections.title: Three families of vector spaces

parts.title: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$
parts.md: Addition and scaling are componentwise: $(1,2)+(3,-1)=(4,1)$ and $2(1,2)=(2,4)$. The zero vector is $(0,\dots,0)$.

parts.title: Matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$
parts.md: Fix the shape $m\times n$ and use matrix addition and scalar multiplication. The zero vector is the zero matrix of that shape.

parts.title: Continuous functions $C(\mathbb{R})$
parts.md:
Operations are pointwise: $(f+g)(t)=f(t)+g(t)$ and $(cf)(t)=c\,f(t)$. The zero vector is the function that is $0$ for every $t$, and the negative of $f$ is $-f$.

For $f(t)=t^2$ and $g(t)=1-t$:

$$(3f-2g)(t)=3t^2-2(1-t)=3t^2+2t-2$$

sections.intro: The same ten rules cover all three.
sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] The zero vector of $C(\mathbb{R})$ is the function $0$, **not** the constant function $1$. The zero vector must leave every function unchanged under addition.

sections.title: Worked example: the subspace test

parts.title: Closed under scaling?
parts.md: For $(x,y)\in W$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$: $cx+cy=c(x+y)=c\cdot0=0$, so $c(x,y)\in W$.

parts.title: Conclusion
parts.md: All three conditions hold, so $W$ is a subspace. Geometrically it is the line $y=-x$ through the origin.

sections.intro: A subset $W$ of a vector space is a **subspace** if it contains $0$ and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; the other axioms are inherited. Is $W=\{(x,y):x+y=0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ a subspace?

sections.title: Three ways a set can fail the test

parts.title: No zero vector
parts.md: $\{(x,y):x+y=1\}$ is a line that misses the origin, so $0\notin W$. This is the quickest check.

parts.title: Not closed under scaling
parts.md: $\{(x,y):x\ge0\}$ contains $0$ and is closed under addition, but $(-1)\cdot(1,0)=(-1,0)$ leaves the set.

parts.title: Not closed under addition
parts.md: $\{(x,y):xy=0\}$ (the two axes) contains $0$ and is closed under scaling, but $(1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1)$ has $xy=1\neq0$.

sections.intro: Each of the three conditions can fail on its own, so you must check all three.
sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] Every subspace contains $0$; failing that single test already settles the question.

sections.title: Worked example: is the map linear?

parts.title: Quick necessary test
parts.md: Compute $T(0)$. If it is not $0$, stop: $T$ is not linear. If it is $0$, you still have to check the two conditions.

parts.title: Homogeneity for $S$
parts.md:
$$S(cu)=(cx_1+cy_1,\ 2cx_1-cy_1)=c\,(x_1+y_1,\ 2x_1-y_1)=cS(u)$$

Both conditions hold for all $u,v,c$, so $S$ is linear.

parts.title: A map that fails homogeneity
parts.md:
$R(x,y)=(xy,\ x)$ has $R(0)=0$ but

$$R(2,2)=(4,2)\quad\text{while}\quad 2R(1,1)=2(1,1)=(2,2)$$

One counterexample is enough: $R$ is not linear.

parts.title: A translation
parts.md: $T(x,y)=(x,\ y+2)$ has $T(0,0)=(0,2)\neq(0,0)$, so it is not linear.

sections.intro: A map $T:V\to W$ is **linear** if $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$ (additivity) and $T(cu)=cT(u)$ (homogeneity) for all vectors and scalars. Equivalently $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$. Every linear map sends $0$ to $0$.
sections.outro: **Back to the prediction:** $T(x,y)=(x+1,y)$ looks simple but $T(0,0)=(1,0)\neq 0$, so it is not linear. Every matrix map $x\mapsto Ax$ is linear because $A(u+v)=Au+Av$ and $A(cu)=cAu$.

sections.title: Worked example: the standard matrix of a linear map

parts.title: Apply T to the basis vectors
Use them as columns
parts.md:
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$$

Why: the images are the **columns**, not the rows.

parts.title: Test it
parts.md: $T(1,2)=(2-2,\ 1+6)=(0,7)$ and $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\7\end{pmatrix}$. Both agree.

parts.title: A map given by its values on a basis
parts.md:
A linear $T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^3$ with $T(e_1)=(1,0,2)$ and $T(e_2)=(0,1,-1)$ has the $3\times2$ matrix

$$\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$$

and $T(3,-2)=3T(e_1)-2T(e_2)=(3,0,6)+(0,-2,2)=(3,-2,8)$. Knowing $T$ on a basis determines $T$ everywhere.

sections.intro: Every linear map $T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ is multiplication by a matrix, the **standard matrix** $A=[T(e_1)\ \cdots\ T(e_n)]$. The reason: $x=\sum_j x_je_j$, so $T(x)=\sum_j x_jT(e_j)=Ax$. Build the matrix of $T(x,y)=(2x-y,\ x+3y)$.
sections.outro: A map $T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ has an $m\times n$ matrix.

sections.title: Linear versus affine maps

parts.title: Linear: $x\mapsto Ax$
parts.md:
- Sends $0$ to $0$.
- Preserves linear combinations: $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$.

parts.title: Affine: $x\mapsto Ax+b$
parts.md:
- $T(0)=b$, so it is linear **exactly when $b=0$**.
- A translation $x\mapsto x+b$ with $b\neq0$ is the basic nonlinear example.

sections.intro: A fully connected layer of a neural network computes $x\mapsto Wx+b$ followed by a nonlinear function. The $Wx$ part is linear; adding the bias $b$ makes the map affine, and the activation function makes the whole thing nonlinear.

sections.title: Worked example: composition and inverse

parts.title: Compose
parts.md:
$S\circ T$ means: apply $T$ first, then $S$. Its matrix is the product with the rightmost factor acting first:

$$BA=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$$

Check: $S(T(x,y))=S(2x+y,\ x+y)=(3x+2y,\ x+y)$.

parts.title: Is T invertible?
parts.md: $\det A=2\cdot1-1\cdot1=1\neq0$, so $A$ is invertible and so is $T$. The matrix of $T^{-1}$ is $A^{-1}$.

parts.title: Compute $A^{-1}$
parts.md: $$A^{-1}=\frac11\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$$

parts.title: Solve $T(v)=(3,2)$
parts.md:
$$T^{-1}(3,2)=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3-2\\-3+4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$$

Check: $T(1,1)=(2+1,\ 1+1)=(3,2)$. Applying $T$ to your answer must give back the input.

sections.intro: Let $T(x,y)=(2x+y,\ x+y)$ and $S(x,y)=(x+y,\ y)$. Their matrices are $A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.

sections.title: Find the error in this solution

parts.md:
On $C(\mathbb{R})$ define $(Sf)(t)=f(t)+1$. A classmate claims $S$ is linear:

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 1.** $S(f+g)(t)=f(t)+g(t)+1$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 2.** $S(f)(t)+S(g)(t)=(f(t)+1)+(g(t)+1)=f(t)+g(t)+1$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 3.** The two agree, so $S$ is additive; it is linear.

:::Which step is wrong?
**Step 2.** $(f+1)+(g+1)=f+g+2$, not $f+g+1$. So $S(f+g)\neq S(f)+S(g)$ and $S$ is not additive. There is also a one-line check from the zero test: $S(0)(t)=0+1=1$ is the constant function $1$, not the zero function, so $S$ cannot be linear. It is an affine map (a translation in $C(\mathbb{R})$).
:::

sections.title: Common confusions

parts.title: Is every vector a column of numbers?
parts.md: No. In this course a vector is any element of a vector space: a matrix in $M_{m\times n}$ or a function in $C(\mathbb{R})$ qualifies, because addition and scaling obey the same ten rules.

parts.title: If $T(0)=0$, is $T$ linear?
parts.md: Not necessarily. $T(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has $T(0)=0$, but $T(1+1)=4\neq T(1)+T(1)=2$. The zero test can only *refute* linearity.

parts.title: Why bother with function spaces?
parts.md: Many operations on functions are linear maps, for example differentiation on polynomials: $(af+bg)'=af'+bg'$. Treating functions as vectors lets the same tools apply to signals, polynomials and models.

parts.title: Does every linear map have a matrix?
parts.md: Every linear map $\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ has a standard matrix whose columns are $T(e_1),\dots,T(e_n)$. For other vector spaces you get a matrix after choosing a basis.

sections.title: Practice with Python

parts.md:
Test the ideas numerically. Build the standard matrix by applying the map to the columns of the identity, then test linearity numerically. ```html 
import numpy as np

def T(v):
    x, y = v
    return np.array([2*x - y, x + 3*y])

E = np.eye(2)
A = np.column_stack([T(E[:, j]) for j in range(2)])   # columns are T(e_j)
print(A)

v = np.array([1., 2.])
print("T(v) =", T(v), " A @ v =", A @ v)                # the same vector

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u, w = rng.normal(size=2), rng.normal(size=2)
a, b = 2.5, -1.5
print(np.allclose(T(a*u + b*w), a*T(u) + b*T(w)))      # T(au + bw) = aT(u) + bT(w)
``` **Output** ```html 
[[ 2. -1.]
 [ 1.  3.]]
T(v) = [0. 7.]  A @ v = [0. 7.]
True
``` A numerical test can **refute** linearity (one counterexample is enough) but it can never prove it: for a proof you need the algebra for all vectors. ```html 
import numpy as np

def R(v):                      # (x, y) -> (xy, x), not linear
    x, y = v
    return np.array([x*y, x])

def Tr(v):                     # translation (x, y) -> (x, y + 2), not linear
    x, y = v
    return np.array([x, y + 2])

zero = np.zeros(2)
print("R(0) =", R(zero), " Tr(0) =", Tr(zero))   # T(0) must be 0 for a linear map

u = np.array([1., 1.])
print("R(2u) =", R(2*u), " 2R(u) =", 2*R(u))     # homogeneity fails for R

A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 1.]])                # matrix of T(x, y) = (2x + y, x + y)
print("T^-1(3, 2) =", np.linalg.solve(A, [3., 2.]))
``` **Output** ```html 
R(0) = [0. 0.]  Tr(0) = [0. 2.]
R(2u) = [4. 2.]  2R(u) = [2. 2.]
T^-1(3, 2) = [1. 1.]
```

flashcards.title: Flashcards · Vector spaces and linear mappings

items.meaning: A nonempty set with addition and real scalar multiplication satisfying ten rules: closure under + and ·, commutativity, associativity, zero vector, additive inverses, two distributive laws, c(du) = (cd)u, 1u = u.
The vector 0 with u + 0 = u for every u. In C(ℝ) it is the function that is 0 for every t (not the constant 1).
ℝⁿ (componentwise), the space M(m × n) of matrices of a fixed shape, and the continuous functions C(ℝ) with pointwise operations.
A subset W is a subspace if it contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
items.example: {(x, y): x + y = 0} is a subspace; {(x, y): x + y = 1} is not (no zero).

items.meaning: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u); equivalently T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v).
Every linear map has T(0) = 0. If T(0) ≠ 0, T is not linear; if T(0) = 0 you still need to check both conditions.
items.example: T(x) = x + b with b ≠ 0 is not linear.

items.meaning: A = [T(e₁) … T(eₙ)]: the j-th column is the image of the j-th standard basis vector; T(x) = Ax.
x ↦ Ax + b. It is linear exactly when b = 0.
items.note: A neural-network layer Wx + b is affine.

items.meaning: The matrix of S ∘ T is BA (T acts first). T is invertible iff its matrix A is invertible, and the matrix of T⁻¹ is A⁻¹.

summary: A vector space is any set with addition and scalar multiplication obeying the ten axioms; Rⁿ, matrices of a fixed shape and continuous functions are examples.
A subset is a subspace if it contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; failing any one of the three means it is not.
A map is linear if T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u); every linear map sends 0 to 0, so T(0) ≠ 0 proves a map is not linear.
Every linear map Rⁿ → Rᵐ is x ↦ Ax with A = [T(e₁) … T(eₙ)]; the images of the basis vectors are the columns.
x ↦ Ax + b is affine and linear only if b = 0; composition corresponds to matrix products and T⁻¹ to A⁻¹.

quiz.title: Quiz · Vector Spaces and Linear Mappings

questions.explanation: Add component by component: $1+2=3$, $-2+4=2$ and $3+(-1)=2$. Addition in a vector space is not componentwise multiplication.

questions.prompt: What is the zero vector in the vector space $C(\mathbb{R})$ of continuous real functions?
questions.explanation: The zero vector must leave every function unchanged under pointwise addition: $f+0=f$. Only the function that is $0$ at every $t$ does that. The constant function $1$ would change $f$ into $f+1$.

questions.prompt: Let $T(x) = x + (1, -2)^\top$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which value of $T(0)$ shows that $T$ is not linear?
questions.explanation: Substituting gives $T(0)=0+(1,-2)^\top=(1,-2)^\top\neq 0$. Every linear map sends $0$ to $0$, so this translation fails a necessary condition and cannot be linear.

questions.prompt: For $f(t) = t^2$ and $g(t) = 1 - t$ in $C(\mathbb{R})$, what is $(2f - g)(t)$?
questions.explanation: Function operations are pointwise: $(2f-g)(t)=2t^2-(1-t)=2t^2-1+t=2t^2+t-1$. The minus sign applies to both terms of $g$.

questions.prompt: What is the standard matrix of $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$, $T(x, y) = (x + 2y,\ 3x - y)$?
questions.explanation: The first column is $T(1,0)=(1,3)^\top$ and the second is $T(0,1)=(2,-1)^\top$. Placing these as columns gives $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}$; writing them as rows gives the transpose (option C).

questions.prompt: Which map from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is linear?
questions.explanation: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ is multiplication by $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so it is linear. The translation $(x+1,y)$ fails $T(0)=0$; the square $(x^2,y)$ fails additivity; and the absolute value $(|x|,y)$ fails homogeneity for negative scalars.

questions.prompt: A linear map has $T(e_1) = (1, 2)^\top$, $T(e_2) = (-1, 3)^\top$. What is $T(2, -1)$?
questions.explanation: Linearity gives $T(2e_1-e_2)=2T(e_1)-T(e_2)=2(1,2)^\top-(-1,3)^\top=(2+1,\ 4-3)^\top=(3,1)^\top$. The negative coefficient applies to both coordinates of $T(e_2)$.

questions.prompt: On $C(\mathbb{R})$, define $(Sf)(t) = f(t) + f(0)$. Which function satisfies $(Sf)(t) = t^2 + 1$ for every real $t$?
questions.explanation: Evaluate at $t=0$: $2f(0)=1$, so $f(0)=\tfrac12$. Then $f(t)=t^2+1-f(0)=t^2+\tfrac12$. It is continuous, and $f(t)+f(0)=t^2+\tfrac12+\tfrac12=t^2+1$ for every $t$.

questions.prompt: A linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $T(1, 1) = 2(1, 1)$ and $T(1, -1) = -(1, -1)$. What is $T^{-1}(3, 1)$?
questions.explanation: The vectors $v_1=(1,1)$ and $v_2=(1,-1)$ are independent and $T$ multiplies them by the nonzero numbers $2$ and $-1$, so $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}$ divides by those numbers. Write $(3,1)=2v_1+v_2$. Then $T^{-1}(3,1)=\tfrac22v_1+\tfrac1{-1}v_2=v_1-v_2=(0,2)$. Check: $T(0,2)=T(v_1-v_2)=2v_1+v_2=(3,1)$. Option C is $T(3,1)$, the map applied instead of its inverse.

questions.prompt: The set $\{(x, y) : x \geq 0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
questions.explanation: False. It contains $0$ and is closed under addition, but not under scalar multiplication: $(-1)\cdot(1,0)=(-1,0)$ has $x\lt 0$. All three conditions must hold.

questions.prompt: Which subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a subspace?
questions.explanation: Only $x+y+z=0$ passes: it contains $0$, and sums and scalar multiples of solutions are again solutions. $x+y+z=1$ misses $0$; $z\geq0$ fails scaling by $-1$; $xyz=0$ (the union of the three coordinate planes) fails addition: $(1,1,0)+(0,0,1)=(1,1,1)$.

questions.prompt: $T:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is linear. Enter the shape of its standard matrix as $m\times n$.
questions.explanation: The standard matrix has one column $T(e_j)$ for each of the $3$ input coordinates, and each column has $2$ entries (it lies in $\mathbb{R}^2$). So the matrix is $2\times3$.

questions.prompt: $T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is linear with $T(e_1)=(1,0,2)^\top$ and $T(e_2)=(0,1,-1)^\top$. Enter the **third** coordinate of $T(3,-2)$.
questions.explanation: $T(3,-2)=3T(e_1)-2T(e_2)=3(1,0,2)-2(0,1,-1)=(3,-2,6+2)=(3,-2,8)$. The third coordinate is $8$. The negative coefficient applies to the whole vector $T(e_2)$, including its third coordinate $-1$.

questions.prompt: If $T(0)=0$, then $T$ is linear.
questions.explanation: False. $T(0)=0$ is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. $T(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has $T(0)=0$, yet $T(1+1)=4\neq T(1)+T(1)=2$. To prove linearity you must check additivity and homogeneity for all vectors.

modules.title: Part II — Calculus and Optimization
modules.description: Functions, exponentials and logarithms; derivatives, the chain rule and marginal effects; partial derivatives and the gradient; optimization and gradient descent. Five class hours that take you from a model's prediction rule to the algorithm that trains it.

lessons.title: Part II materials: lecture notes and slides
lessons.description: What the Part II lecture notes and slides contain, which sections go with which topic, a study routine, and the notation used throughout.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this page you can:
objectives: Say what the lecture notes and slides of Part II contain and which sections belong to which topic
Follow a study routine that combines slides, lesson, quiz, exercises and flashcards
Read the notation (x, y, ŷ, b, w, θ, r, η) used in all four topics
lessons.body:
Part II turns one question into a method. A model predicts $\hat y=b+wx$. If the prediction misses its target, how should we change $b$ and $w$? A **derivative** measures how one change affects the error, a **gradient** collects these effects for all parameters, and **gradient descent** uses them to choose the next parameters. The four topics of this module build that argument step by step.

Two PDFs accompany the module. This page tells you what is in them and how to use them with the topic lessons.

## What the PDFs contain

| Material | What it is | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Lecture notes** (20 pages) | The four lessons in full: definitions, derivations, worked examples you can follow by hand, then 16 exercises (pp. 16–17) and their solutions (pp. 18–20). | Read the section for a topic after the lesson, to see the full derivations. Attempt the exercises before you open the solutions. |
| **Lecture slides** (37 slides) | The same four lessons as an outline, with the key definitions, one example per idea, and the animated gradient-descent run. | Skim the matching slides before you start a topic so you know where the lesson is heading. |

The 50 practice questions that go with the notes (20 easy, 18 medium, 12 hard) are built into the quizzes of this module, sorted by topic, so you do not need a separate file for them.

## Which part belongs to which topic

| Topic | Lecture notes | Slides | Exercises |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 · Functions, exponentials and logarithms | Section 1 (pp. 2–4) | 2–5 | 1, 2, 11 |
| 7 · Derivatives, chain rule and marginal effects | Section 2 (pp. 4–7) | 6–13 | 3, 4, 5, 12 |
| 8 · Partial derivatives and the gradient | Section 3 (pp. 8–11) | 14–22 | 6, 7, 13, 14 |
| 9 · Optimization and gradient descent | Section 4 (pp. 11–16) | 23–37 | 8, 9, 10, 15, 16 |

## A good routine for each topic

1. **Skim** the matching slides (5 minutes).
2. Work through the **lesson**. Attempt every worked example yourself before you reveal the next step, and answer each "predict" prompt in writing.
3. Take the **quiz**. Rate your confidence before you see each answer.
4. Read the matching **lecture-notes section**, then try the **exercises**.
5. Review the lesson **flashcards** the next day, and again a week later.

> [!meo] The notes and the lessons use the same examples on purpose (the line $\hat y=b+wx$ fitted to the points $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$, the loss $(x-2)^2$, the function $b^2+3bw+2w^2$). When a derivation in the notes feels too fast, find the same example in the lesson and step through it slowly.

## Notation used throughout

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $n,\ m$ | Dimension of an input or parameter vector, and sample size |
| $x_i,\ y_i,\ \hat y_i$ | Feature, observed target and prediction for observation $i$ |
| $b,\ w,\ \theta$ | Intercept, slope, and the parameter vector $\theta=(b,w)^\top$ |
| $r_i$ | Residual $\hat y_i-y_i$; a positive residual means overprediction |
| $\eta_k$ | Learning rate at iteration $k$ |

lessons.title: Topic 6 · Functions, Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
lessons.description: Functions, domains and ranges; affine models and the two roles of their inputs; exponentials, logarithms and the sigmoid, with growth and threshold problems solved on the log scale.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
objectives: Find the natural domain and range of simple functions such as ln(5 − 2x) and 3 + e^(−x)
Distinguish affine from nonlinear functions and read the slope as a constant rate of change
Explain the two roles of a model's inputs: features in prediction, parameters in training
Use exp and ln as inverses and apply the three logarithm rules, including knowing that no rule exists for a sum
Solve exponential-growth and sigmoid-threshold problems by working on the log or log-odds scale
lessons.body:
Every model you will train in this course is a **function with adjustable parameters**. A line $\hat y=b+wx$ turns a feature into a prediction, a sigmoid turns a score into a probability, and a loss turns a prediction error into one number to make small. Before we study how a function *changes* (Topics 7–9), we need to be fluent with the functions themselves: what they accept, what they return, and the two that dominate machine learning, the exponential and the logarithm.

> [!ghi-nho] A function $f:D\to Y$ assigns **exactly one** value $f(x)\in Y$ to every $x\in D$. $D$ is the **domain**, $Y$ is the **codomain**, and the **range** $f(D)=\{f(x):x\in D\}$ is the set of values the function actually takes.

:::Before you read on, predict
A model gives the probability $p(x)=\sigma(2x-4)$, and an action is triggered when $p(x)\geq 0.8$. At $x=2$ the score $2x-4$ equals $0$. Without a calculator, do you expect the cut-off to lie above or below $x=2$? Write down your guess and a one-line reason. You will compute the exact cut-off in the sigmoid example below.
:::

sections.title: Four words to keep apart

parts.md: The inputs the formula or the problem allows. $\ln(x-2)$ has domain $(2,\infty)$ because its argument must be positive. A cost $C(q)=100+5q$ has natural domain $[0,\infty)$ because a quantity cannot be negative.
parts.title: Domain

parts.md: The set $Y$ the outputs are declared to live in. For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ it is $\mathbb R$, even if not every real number is reached.
parts.title: Codomain

parts.md: The values actually taken, $f(D)$. For $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ the range is $[0,\infty)$. For $C(q)=100+5q$ with $q\ge 0$ it is $[100,\infty)$.
parts.title: Range

parts.md: When only a formula is given, the set of real inputs for which it is defined: no division by zero, and the argument of a logarithm strictly positive.
parts.title: Natural real domain

sections.intro: Most mistakes with domains and ranges come from mixing these four ideas up.

sections.title: Affine and nonlinear functions

parts.md:
- Intercept $f(0)=b$ and **constant slope** $w$.
- For any increment $h$: $f(x+h)-f(x)=wh$. The same step changes the output by the same amount at every starting point.
- Example: $f(x)=2+3x$ has $f(0)=2$ and $f(2)-f(1)=3$.
- In linear algebra it is a *linear map* only when $b=0$; machine learning nevertheless calls $b+wx$ a **linear model**.
parts.title: Affine: f(x) = b + wx

parts.md:
- A one-unit increase in $x$ changes $f$ by $2x+1$.
- Starting at $x=1$: $f$ rises by $3$. Starting at $x=10$: it rises by $21$.
- The effect **depends on the starting point**. Measuring that changing rate exactly is the job of the derivative (Topic 7).
parts.title: Nonlinear: f(x) = x²

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] The slope of an affine function is the one rate that never changes. For every other function the slope varies from point to point, and that is why we need calculus.

sections.title: Worked example: one model, two roles

parts.md:
$$f_\theta(x)=b+wx,\qquad \theta=(b,w)^\top .$$

Why: $\theta$ collects the adjustable **parameters**; $x$ is the input **feature**.
parts.title: Write the rule

parts.md:
With $(b,w)=(1,2)$ and $x=3$: $f_\theta(3)=1+2\cdot 3=7$.

With $(b,w)=(0,1)$ and $x=3$: $f_\theta(3)=0+1\cdot 3=3$.

Why: in a **prediction** problem the parameters are fixed and the feature varies.
parts.title: Prediction: fix the parameters, vary x

parts.md:
Take one observation $(x,y)=(3,7)$ and measure the error of the model by $L(b,w)=(b+3w-7)^2$. Then

$$L(1,2)=(1+6-7)^2=0,\qquad L(0,1)=(0+3-7)^2=16 .$$

Why: now $x$ and $y$ are fixed numbers and $(b,w)$ are the **inputs** of $L$. Fitting the line means choosing $(b,w)$ to make $L$ small, a function of the parameters that Topic 9 minimises.
parts.title: Training: fix the data, vary the parameters

sections.intro: The same formula is used in two different ways. Reveal the steps one at a time.

sections.title: Exponentials and logarithms

parts.md: A function $a^x$ with base $a>0$, $a\ne1$ has domain $\mathbb R$ and range $(0,\infty)$. Increasing $x$ by 1 multiplies the value by $a$. It rises if $a>1$ and falls if $0\lt a\lt1$. The base $e\approx2.71828$ is the convenient one in calculus because $(e^x)'=e^x$.
parts.title: Exponential

parts.md: $\ln:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse of $x\mapsto e^x$: $\ln y=x\iff e^x=y$ for $y>0$. The graphs of $e^x$ and $\ln x$ are mirror images in the line $y=x$; the points $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ show inputs and outputs swapping places.
parts.title: Natural logarithm

parts.md: $$\ln(e^x)=x,\qquad e^{\ln y}=y\ (y>0),\qquad \ln 1=0,\qquad \ln e=1 .$$
parts.title: Inverse identities

parts.md:
For $u,v>0$ and any real $c$:

$$\ln(uv)=\ln u+\ln v,\qquad \ln\frac uv=\ln u-\ln v,\qquad \ln(u^c)=c\ln u .$$
parts.title: Three rules

sections.outro:
> [!canh-bao] The rules cover **products, quotients and powers**. There is **no rule for a sum**: $\ln(1+1)=\ln2\approx0.693$ but $\ln1+\ln1=0$. In general $\ln(a+b)\ne\ln a+\ln b$.

Logarithms put equal *ratios* at equal distances: $1,10,100$ are equally spaced on a log scale because each step adds $\ln10$. A log transformation is undefined for zeros and negative values, and when you fit a model to $\ln Y$ its residuals are measured on the log scale, so the fitting criterion changes.

sections.title: Worked example: compound growth on the log scale

parts.md:
$$A(2)=200\,e^{2k}=242\ \Longrightarrow\ e^{2k}=\frac{242}{200}=1.21 .$$

Why: dividing isolates the exponential. $1.21$ is the growth factor over two years.
parts.title: Use the second data point

parts.md:
$$2k=\ln1.21\ \Longrightarrow\ k=\tfrac12\ln1.21=\ln1.1\approx0.09531 .$$

Why: $\ln(e^{2k})=2k$, and $1.21=1.1^2$, so the power rule gives $\ln1.21=2\ln1.1$.
parts.title: Take logarithms to solve for k

parts.md: $$e^{k}=1.1\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{output grows by } 10\%\text{ per year.}$$
parts.title: Convert to an annual percentage

parts.md:
$$\ln A(t)=\ln 200+t\ln 1.1 .$$

Why: on the log scale exponential growth is a straight line in $t$ with intercept $\ln200$ and slope $k$. This is why 'take logs, then fit a line' works.
parts.title: Write the log-scale model

parts.md: $$e^{kt}=2\ \Longrightarrow\ t=\frac{\ln 2}{k}\approx7.27\text{ years.}$$
parts.title: Doubling time

sections.intro: A firm's output follows $A(t)=A_0e^{kt}$ with $t$ in years. It produces 200 units initially and 242 units two years later. Find $A_0$, $k$, the annual percentage increase and the log-scale equation.
sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] A **5% annual rise** corresponds to the continuous rate $k=\ln1.05\approx0.04879$. A **continuous rate of 0.05** gives an annual rise of $e^{0.05}-1\approx5.13\%$.

sections.title: The sigmoid in six facts

parts.md:
An affine score $z=b+wx$ can be any real number, but a probability must lie in $(0,1)$. The **logistic function** or **sigmoid** converts one into the other:

$$p=\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} .$$

- The denominator exceeds 1, so $0\lt\sigma(z)\lt1$ strictly: it never reaches 0 or 1.
- $\sigma(0)=1/2$.
- $\sigma$ is increasing, because a larger $z$ makes $e^{-z}$ and the denominator smaller.
- As $z\to-\infty$, $p\to0$. As $z\to+\infty$, $p\to1$. The curve is steepest at $z=0$ and flattens at both ends.
- The **odds** of a probability are $p/(1-p)$ and $\dfrac{p}{1-p}=e^{z}\iff \ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}=z$. So the inverse of $\sigma$ is the **log-odds**.
- One extra unit of score multiplies the odds by $e$. The scores $-\ln3,\ 0,\ \ln3$ give the probabilities $1/4,\ 1/2,\ 3/4$.

sections.title: Worked example: finding a decision threshold

parts.md: $$p(x)=\sigma(2x-4),\qquad \text{act when } p(x)\ge 0.8 .$$
parts.title: State the rule

parts.md:
$$\text{odds}=\frac{0.8}{1-0.8}=4 .$$

Why: $p/(1-p)=e^{z}$, so the threshold in odds is 4.
parts.title: Convert the probability to odds

parts.md:
$$z=\ln 4\approx1.386 .$$

Why: the inverse of the sigmoid is the log-odds. Using $0.8$ or $\ln0.8$ here is the classic slip.
parts.title: Convert the odds to a score

parts.md:
$$p(x)\ge0.8\iff 2x-4\ge\ln4 .$$

Why: $\sigma$ is increasing, so it preserves the direction of an inequality. Here the inner score $2x-4$ is also increasing in $x$.
parts.title: Translate the condition

parts.md: $$x\ge 2+\tfrac12\ln4\approx2.693 .$$
parts.title: Solve for x

parts.md: For a probability threshold of $1/2$ the score threshold is $0$, so the cut-off would be $x=2$. Asking for a higher probability, $0.8$, pushes the cut-off **above** $x=2$.
parts.title: Check against the prediction prompt

sections.intro: Press the step button to reveal each line.

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
Each solution below contains **one** wrong step. Find it before you open the answer.

**Item 1.** A student finds the domain of $f(x)=\ln(4-3x)$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 1.** The argument must be positive: $4-3x>0$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 2.** Subtract 4: $-3x>-4$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 3.** Divide by $-3$: $x>\tfrac43$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 4.** The domain is $\left(\tfrac43,\infty\right)$.

:::Which step is wrong?
**Step 3.** Dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality, so $x\lt\tfrac43$ and the domain is $\left(-\infty,\tfrac43\right)$. Check with numbers: $x=0$ gives $\ln4$, which is defined, but $x=2$ gives $\ln(-2)$, which is not.
:::

**Item 2.** A student simplifies $\ln(x+3)-\ln x$ for $x>0$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 1.** A difference of logarithms is a logarithm of a difference: $\ln(x+3)-\ln x=\ln\big((x+3)-x\big)$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 2.** Simplify inside: $\ln 3$.

:::Which step is wrong?
**Step 1.** The quotient rule turns a difference of logs into the log of a *quotient*: $\ln(x+3)-\ln x=\ln\dfrac{x+3}{x}$. Test it with $x=1$: $\ln4-\ln1\approx1.386$, whereas $\ln3\approx1.099$.
:::

sections.title: Questions that come up

parts.md: In linear algebra a linear map must satisfy $f(0)=0$, so only $b=0$ qualifies; $b+wx$ is an *affine* function. Machine learning calls it a linear model because it is linear in the parameters and in the features once the constant feature 1 is included. Both uses are common, so check which one a text means.
parts.title: Is b + wx a linear function?

parts.md: The codomain is where the outputs are *allowed* to be; the range is where they *actually* land. $f(x)=x^2$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$ has codomain $\mathbb R$ but range $[0,\infty)$.
parts.title: What is the difference between codomain and range?

parts.md: Because $(e^x)'=e^x$ and $(\ln x)'=1/x$ are the simplest derivatives (Topic 7). Other bases differ only by a constant: $\log_{10}x=\ln x/\ln 10$.
parts.title: Why the natural logarithm and not log base 10?

parts.md: They cannot be logged directly. Your options are to model the target on its original scale, or to transform it in a way you can justify. Whichever you choose, remember that fitting $\ln Y$ measures residuals on the log scale, so the loss you minimise is different from the one on the original scale.
parts.title: What if my data contain zeros or negative values?

parts.md: Never. For every finite score the denominator is greater than 1, so $\sigma(z)\lt1$, and $e^{-z}\gt0$ gives $\sigma(z)\gt0$. It only approaches the ends as $|z|$ grows.
parts.title: Does the sigmoid ever reach exactly 0 or 1?

sections.title: Practice with Python

parts.md:
Run these snippets yourself and change the numbers. The first reproduces the growth example; the second checks the sigmoid cut-off. ```html
Python
import numpy as np

A0, A2 = 200, 242                  # output now and two years later
k = np.log(A2 / A0) / 2            # from A(2) = A0 * exp(2k)
print("k =", round(k, 5))
print("annual factor e^k =", round(np.exp(k), 4))
print("doubling time ln2/k =", round(np.log(2) / k, 2), "years")

# there is no rule for a sum inside a logarithm
print(np.log(2 + 3), np.log(2) + np.log(3))
Output
k = 0.09531
annual factor e^k = 1.1
doubling time ln2/k = 7.27 years
1.6094379124341003 1.791759469228055
``` ```html
Python
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

x_star = 2 + 0.5 * np.log(4)               # cut-off from the worked example
print("cut-off x* =", round(x_star, 3))
print("p(x*) =", round(float(sigmoid(2 * x_star - 4)), 4))
for z in (-np.log(3), 0, np.log(3)):       # scores -ln 3, 0, ln 3
    print(f"sigma({z:+.4f}) = {sigmoid(z):.2f}")
Output
cut-off x* = 2.693
p(x*) = 0.8
sigma(-1.0986) = 0.25
sigma(+0.0000) = 0.50
sigma(+1.0986) = 0.75
``` Notice that `np.log` is the **natural** logarithm. The last line of the first snippet shows $\ln 5\ne\ln2+\ln3$ in numbers.

items.meaning: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. The range is the set of outputs actually taken.
items.example: f(x) = x² on ℝ has range [0, ∞).

items.meaning: The real inputs for which a formula is defined.
items.example: ln(x − 2) needs x − 2 > 0, so the domain is (2, ∞).

items.meaning: f(x) = b + wx: intercept b and constant slope w, so f(x + h) − f(x) = wh at every x.
items.example: In ML, b + wx is called a linear model.

items.meaning: eˣ has domain ℝ and range (0, ∞): always positive, never 0.
ln is the inverse of eˣ: ln y = x ⇔ eˣ = y for y > 0. Also ln(eˣ) = x, ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1.
ln(uv) = ln u + ln v; ln(u/v) = ln u − ln v; ln(uᶜ) = c ln u. There is no rule for ln(u + v).

items.term: Exponential growth on the log scale
items.meaning: A(t) = A₀e^(kt) gives ln A(t) = ln A₀ + kt, a straight line with slope k. Doubling time = ln 2 / k.
items.example: A rise of 10% per year has k = ln 1.1 ≈ 0.0953.

items.meaning: σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) maps any score to a probability strictly between 0 and 1; σ(0) = 1/2 and σ is increasing.
odds = p/(1 − p). The log-odds ln(p/(1 − p)) is the inverse of σ. One unit of score multiplies the odds by e.
items.example: p = 3/4 has odds 3 and score ln 3.

summary: A function has a domain, a codomain and a range; read domains and ranges from the formula and keep endpoints that are never reached out of the set.
An affine function b + wx has one constant rate, the slope w; every other function has a slope that varies, which is why we need derivatives.
In a model the same formula plays two roles: features vary in prediction, parameters vary in training.
ln and exp are inverses. The log rules cover products, quotients and powers, never sums.
On the log scale exponential growth is linear (slope k); on the log-odds scale the sigmoid is linear in the score. Solve thresholds there, then convert back.

questions.prompt: What is the natural real domain of $f(x)=\ln(5-2x)$?
questions.explanation: The logarithm needs a strictly positive argument: $5-2x>0$. Subtracting 5 and dividing by $-2$ reverses the inequality, so $x\lt 5/2$. The endpoint $5/2$ is excluded because $\ln 0$ is undefined. Check: $x=0$ gives $\ln 5$ (fine), $x=3$ gives $\ln(-1)$ (undefined).

questions.prompt: What is the range of $f(x)=3+e^{-x}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$?
questions.explanation: As $x$ runs over $\mathbb R$, $e^{-x}$ takes every strictly positive value, never 0 and never a negative value. Adding 3 shifts the range up by 3: $f$ takes every value greater than 3 and never 3 itself, so the range is $(3,\infty)$.

questions.prompt: A model predicts $\hat y=4-3x$. What is the change in the prediction when the feature $x$ increases by 2 units?
questions.explanation: The slope is $-3$, so the change is $(-3)(2)=-6$ at any starting value of $x$, because an affine function has a constant rate. The slope $-3$ is a rate, not a change; and the sign matters: the prediction falls.

questions.prompt: Which expression equals $\ln(2e^{3})$?
questions.explanation: The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms: $\ln(2e^3)=\ln2+\ln(e^3)=\ln2+3$. The exponent 3 belongs to $e$ only, so it multiplies $\ln e=1$, not $\ln2$. Option D, $\ln5=\ln(2+3)$, would need a rule for sums, and none exists.

questions.prompt: Output follows $A(t)=60e^{kt}$, with $t$ in years. If $A(3)=96$, how many years does it take for output to double from its initial level?
questions.explanation: $60e^{3k}=96$ gives $e^{3k}=96/60=8/5$, so $k=\tfrac13\ln\tfrac85$. Doubling means $e^{kt}=2$, hence $t=\ln2/k=\dfrac{3\ln2}{\ln(8/5)}\approx4.42$ years. Option B uses the relative increase $3/5$ instead of the growth factor $8/5$ ($\ln(3/5)$ is negative, giving a negative time). Options C and D invert the ratio; C would give about 2.0 years, less than the 3 years it took to grow by only 60%.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x)=4+x^2$ on $x\le 0$. What is $f^{-1}(y)$ for $y\ge 4$?
questions.explanation: Solving $y=4+x^2$ gives $x^2=y-4$, so $x=\pm\sqrt{y-4}$. The restriction $x\le0$ selects the non-positive root: $f^{-1}(y)=-\sqrt{y-4}$. Check: $f(-2)=8$ and $f^{-1}(8)=-\sqrt4=-2$. The positive root (option C) would be the inverse of $f$ restricted to $x\ge 0$.

questions.prompt: Let $p(x)=\sigma(3-2x)$, where $\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$. For which $x$ does $p(x)\ge 3/4$?
questions.explanation: The odds at $p=3/4$ are $\frac{3/4}{1/4}=3$, so the threshold score is $\ln3$. Since $\sigma$ is increasing, $p(x)\ge3/4$ means $3-2x\ge\ln3$. Subtract 3 and divide by $-2$, reversing the inequality: $x\le(3-\ln3)/2\approx0.95$. The score $3-2x$ decreases as $x$ grows, so the condition is an upper bound on $x$; option D has the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: A probability model is $p(x)=\sigma(b+wx)$, with $\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$. If $p(1)=1/5$ and $p(3)=4/5$, what is $p(4)$?
questions.explanation: The log-odds are affine in $x$. At $x=1$ the odds are $\frac{1/5}{4/5}=\frac14$, so the log-odds are $-\ln4$; at $x=3$ they are $+\ln4$. The slope is $\frac{\ln4-(-\ln4)}{3-1}=\ln4$, so at $x=4$ the log-odds are $2\ln4$ and the odds are $16$. Hence $p(4)=\frac{16}{1+16}=\frac{16}{17}$. Extrapolating the probabilities themselves does not work: only the log-odds are linear in $x$.

questions.prompt: A model uses $p(x)=\sigma(2x-4)$ and acts when $p(x)\ge 0.8$. Which condition on the **score** $2x-4$ is equivalent?
questions.explanation: The score is the log-odds. At $p=0.8$ the odds are $0.8/0.2=4$, so the score threshold is $\ln4\approx1.386$. Using $0.8$, $\ln0.8$ or the odds $4$ itself mixes up probability, odds and log-odds. Solving $2x-4\ge\ln4$ gives $x\ge2+\tfrac12\ln4\approx2.693$.

questions.prompt: For all positive numbers $a$ and $b$, $\ln(a+b)=\ln a+\ln b$.
questions.explanation: False. The rule is $\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$, for a **product**. With $a=b=1$: $\ln 2\approx0.693$ but $\ln1+\ln1=0$. There is no rule for the logarithm of a sum.

questions.prompt: Output follows $A(t)=A_0e^{kt}$ with $A(0)=200$ and $A(2)=242$. By what percentage does output rise each year? Enter a number (percent).
questions.explanation: $e^{2k}=242/200=1.21$, so the annual factor is $e^k=\sqrt{1.21}=1.1$: output rises by $10\%$ per year ($k=\ln1.1\approx0.0953$).

questions.prompt: Match each expression with its value.
questions.explanation: $\ln1=0$, $\ln e=1$, $\ln(e^5)=5$ and $e^{\ln7}=7$ because ln and exp are inverses. The last one uses the quotient rule: $\ln12-\ln4=\ln\frac{12}{4}=\ln3$.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for finding the cut-off of $p(x)=\sigma(2x-4)\ge 0.8$ in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Probability to odds to log-odds gives the score threshold; then, because the sigmoid is increasing, the condition on p becomes the same-direction condition on the score; finally solve the affine inequality for x.
sequence: Convert the threshold probability to odds: 0.8 / 0.2 = 4
Take the logarithm of the odds to get the score threshold: ln 4
Because σ is increasing, require 2x − 4 ≥ ln 4
Solve for x: x ≥ 2 + ½ ln 4 ≈ 2.693

lessons.title: Topic 7 · Derivatives, the Chain Rule and Marginal Effects
lessons.description: Limits and continuity, the derivative as a limit of secant slopes, the basic rules and the chain rule, and marginal effects, with applications to prediction error, cost and the sigmoid.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
objectives: Compute simple limits, including removable 0/0 forms, and decide continuity at a point
Explain a derivative as the limit of secant slopes and as the slope of the tangent line
Differentiate polynomials, exponentials and logarithms and compositions of them with the product and chain rules
Distinguish an average rate, an instantaneous rate and a change, and estimate changes with Δf ≈ f′(a)Δx
Interpret a derivative as a marginal effect, including its sign and units
Use second-order Taylor terms and centered differences to judge the quality of a local approximation
lessons.body:
Training a model means asking one question over and over: *if I nudge this parameter, how much does the loss change?* That sensitivity is a **derivative**. This lesson builds it from limits, shows how to compute it, puts the **chain rule** at the centre (it is the engine behind every gradient you will meet, including the sigmoid loss in Topic 8), and turns the result into something you can interpret: a **marginal effect**.

> [!ghi-nho] The **derivative** of $f$ at $a$ is $f'(a)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$, provided this limit exists as a finite number. It is the local rate of change of $f$ at $a$ and the slope of the tangent line there.

:::Two predictions before you read on
(1) Sketch $f(x)=|x|$. Does its graph have a tangent line at $x=0$? (2) A classmate says the derivative of $(3x+1)^2$ is $2(3x+1)$. Do you agree? Decide on both, with a reason, then check against the lesson.
:::

sections.title: Limits and continuity

parts.md: Suppose $f$ is defined on an open interval around $a$, possibly except at $a$ itself. We write $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ if $f(x)$ can be made as close to $L$ as we like by taking $x$ close enough to $a$, with $x\ne a$. The limit can exist even when $f$ is undefined at $a$.
parts.title: Limit

parts.md: $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)$ uses only $x$ below $a$; $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$ uses only $x$ above $a$. The two-sided limit exists and equals $L$ exactly when **both** one-sided limits equal $L$.
parts.title: One-sided limits

parts.md: $f$ is continuous at $a$ if $f(a)$ is defined and $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$. Three things must agree: the value, the limit, and the fact that the limit exists. $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous at 2 because $\lim_{x\to2}x^2=4=f(2)$.
parts.title: Continuity

sections.title: Worked example: a missing value and a jump

parts.md:
$$f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1\qquad(x\ne1).$$

Why: a limit looks only at $x\ne1$, so the common factor can be cancelled.
parts.title: Cancel the common factor

parts.md: $f(1)$ is not defined, so $f$ is not continuous at 1. Defining $f(1)=2$ fills the hole and makes $f$ continuous there. Any other value leaves the limit at 2 and the function discontinuous.
parts.title: Decide about continuity

parts.md:
Take $g(x)=0$ for $x\lt0$ and $g(x)=1$ for $x\ge0$. Then $\lim_{x\to0^-}g=0$ and $\lim_{x\to0^+}g=1$.

The one-sided limits differ, so $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)$ does not exist, and changing the value $g(0)$ alone cannot repair it.
parts.title: A jump is different from a hole

sections.intro: Two functions that misbehave at a single point, in two different ways.

sections.title: Worked example: from a secant slope to a tangent slope

parts.md:
$$\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}=\frac{(a+h)^2-a^2}{h}.$$

Why: this is the average rate of change between $a$ and $a+h$, and the slope of the **secant** line through the two points.
parts.title: Write the difference quotient for f(x) = x²

parts.md: $$\frac{(a+h)^2-a^2}{h}=\frac{2ah+h^2}{h}=2a+h\qquad(h\ne0).$$
parts.title: Expand the numerator

parts.md: At $a=1$: $f'(1)=2$, so the tangent line is $y=1+2(x-1)$.
parts.title: Read the tangent at a = 1

parts.md:
The secant from $x=1$ to $x=1+h$ has slope $2+h$:

| $h$ | 1 | 0.5 | 0.1 | 0.01 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| secant slope | 3 | 2.5 | 2.1 | 2.01 |

As the second point approaches the first, the slope approaches 2.
parts.title: Watch the secants close in

sections.intro: Derive $f'(a)$ for $f(x)=x^2$ straight from the definition.

sections.title: Average rate and instantaneous rate

parts.md:
- The slope of the **secant** over an interval $[a,b]$: $\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
- For $f(x)=x^2$ on $[1,3]$: $\dfrac{9-1}{2}=4$.
- A *change* in the output divided by the *width* of the input interval.
parts.title: Average rate (secant)

parts.md:
- The slope of the **tangent** at one point: $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$.
- For $f(x)=x^2$: $f'(1)=2$ and $f'(3)=6$.
- Neither equals the average rate 4 over $[1,3]$; the rate varies along the curve.
parts.title: Instantaneous rate (tangent)

sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] A derivative is a **rate** (output units per input unit). To get a **change**, multiply by the step: $\Delta f\approx f'(a)\,\Delta x$. To get an **average rate**, divide a change by the width of the interval.

sections.title: Continuous, differentiable, or neither?

parts.md: Continuous and differentiable at 0, with $f'(0)=0$: the difference quotient is $h$, which tends to 0.
parts.title: x² at 0

parts.md: Continuous but **not** differentiable at 0. The function values approach 0, but the difference quotient is $\dfrac{|h|}{h}$: it equals $-1$ for $h\lt0$ and $+1$ for $h\gt0$. The corner has no single tangent slope.
parts.title: |x| at 0

parts.md: Not continuous at 0 (the one-sided limits differ), so certainly not differentiable.
parts.title: The jump g at 0

parts.md: Undefined at 1, so not continuous there. Defining $f(1)=2$ repairs continuity; the repaired function is then also differentiable at 1.
parts.title: (x² − 1)/(x − 1) at 1

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] **Differentiable at $a$ implies continuous at $a$**: $f(a+h)-f(a)=h\cdot\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$, and if the quotient has a finite limit the product tends to 0. The converse is false: $|x|$ is continuous but not differentiable at 0.

sections.title: Derivative rules

parts.md:
In this table $a,b,c$ are constants and $p$ is a positive integer; the sum, product and quotient rules apply wherever $f$ and $g$ are differentiable.

| Function | Derivative | Note |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ | $0$ | constant |
| $x^p$ | $p\,x^{p-1}$ | power rule |
| $af+bg$ | $af'+bg'$ | linearity |
| $fg$ | $f'g+fg'$ | product rule: both factors vary |
| $f/g$ | $\dfrac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}$ | quotient rule, $g\ne0$ |
| $e^x$ | $e^x$ | |
| $e^{kx}$ | $k\,e^{kx}$ | chain rule |
| $\ln x$ | $\dfrac1x$ | $x\gt0$ |
| $\ln u(x)$ | $\dfrac{u'(x)}{u(x)}$ | chain rule: the proportional rate of change of $u$ |

For example $(xe^x)'=e^x+xe^x$, because **both** factors vary with $x$.

A local approximation follows from the definition. The tangent line at $a$ is $y=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$, and for small $h$

$$f(a+h)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\,h .$$

If $f'(a)\gt0$ a small increase in $x$ raises $f$; if $f'(a)\lt0$ it lowers $f$; if $f'(a)=0$ the linear term vanishes and we need more information.

sections.title: Worked example: four compositions

parts.md:
$$\text{outer } u^2,\ \text{inner } 3x+1:\qquad \frac{d}{dx}(3x+1)^2=2(3x+1)\cdot 3=6(3x+1).$$

Why: the classmate in the prediction prompt forgot the inner factor 3.
parts.title: (3x + 1)²

parts.md: $$\text{outer } e^u,\ \text{inner } 3x-1:\qquad \frac{d}{dx}e^{3x-1}=e^{3x-1}\cdot 3=3e^{3x-1}.$$
parts.title: e^(3x − 1)

parts.md: $$\text{outer } \ln u,\ \text{inner } 1+x^2:\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{1}{1+x^2}\cdot 2x=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.$$
parts.title: ln(1 + x²)

parts.md:
Let $u=1+e^{2x}$. The inner derivative $u'=2e^{2x}$ is itself a chain (outer $e^v$, inner $2x$). Then

$$g'(x)=\frac{u'}{u}=\frac{2e^{2x}}{1+e^{2x}},\qquad g'(0)=\frac{2}{2}=1 .$$

Why: a chain can contain another chain; take it one layer at a time.
parts.title: ln(1 + e^(2x))

sections.intro: The **chain rule**: if $g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$, then $(f\circ g)'(x)=f'(g(x))\,g'(x)$. Evaluate the outer derivative at the current inner value, then multiply by the inner derivative.

sections.title: Worked example: differentiating a squared prediction error

parts.md:
$$\hat y=b+wx,\qquad r=\hat y-y,\qquad \ell(w)=r^2 .$$

Why: $b$, $x$ and $y$ are fixed numbers; only $w$ varies.
parts.title: Set up one observation

parts.md: $$\frac{dr}{dw}=x .$$
parts.title: Inner derivative

parts.md: $$\ell'(w)=2r\,\frac{dr}{dw}=2(b+wx-y)\,x .$$
parts.title: Chain rule

parts.md: The derivative is negative, so raising $w$ lowers the loss. Increasing $w$ by $0.01$ changes the loss by about $-4(0.01)=-0.04$. Exactly: the new residual is $-0.98$ and the loss is $0.9604$, a change of $-0.0396$.
parts.title: Interpret the sign and the size

parts.md: If $x=0$ then $\ell'(w)=0$ for every $w$: this observation's prediction does not depend on $w$, so $w$ cannot reduce its error.
parts.title: An edge case

sections.intro: With both $b$ and $w$ free, this gives the sensitivity along the $w$ coordinate with $b$ held fixed; Topic 8 stacks such coordinate-by-coordinate results into one vector.

sections.title: Worked example: marginal cost and marginal effects

parts.md: $$C'(q)=5+0.2q\quad\text{(money per unit of output).}$$
parts.title: Differentiate the cost

parts.md: $$\Delta C\approx C'(10)\,\Delta q=7(0.2)=1.4 .$$
parts.title: Estimate the cost of 0.2 more units

parts.md: $C(10.2)-C(10)=161.404-160=1.404$. In general $C(10+h)-C(10)=7h+0.1h^2$, and the term $0.1h^2$ is exactly what the tangent approximation leaves out.
parts.title: Compare with the exact change

parts.md: A **marginal effect** is a derivative read in context: *per additional unit of $q$, cost rises by about 7 (money)*. It is a statement about small changes near $q=10$ and its sign and units matter. At $q=20$ the marginal cost is $9$, so the effect depends on where you stand.
parts.title: Say it in words

sections.intro: A cost function $C(q)=100+5q+0.1q^2$ for output $q\ge0$.

sections.title: Worked example: a second-order estimate of a logarithm

parts.md:
$$f(1.1)\approx 0.1+\tfrac12 f''(1)(0.1)^2=0.1-\tfrac12(0.01)=0.095 .$$

Why: the second-order Taylor formula is $f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+\tfrac12f''(a)h^2+o(h^2)$.
parts.title: Add the curvature term

parts.md: The actual value is $\ln1.1\approx0.095310$. The negative curvature ($f''\lt0$) bends the graph below its tangent, which is why the correction moves the estimate down.
parts.title: Compare

sections.intro: At a stationary point $f'(a)=0$, a positive $f''(a)$ gives a strict local minimum and a negative $f''(a)$ a strict local maximum. When $f''(a)=0$ higher-order terms decide: $x^4$ and $x^3$ both have $f'(0)=f''(0)=0$, but only $x^4$ has a minimum there.
sections.outro:
**Checking a derivative from function values.** For $h\gt0$ the forward and centered differences are

$$Q_h^{+}(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},\qquad Q_h^{c}(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a-h)}{2h}.$$

For $f(x)=x^3$ at $a=1$: $Q_h^+=3+3h+h^2$ and $Q_h^c=3+h^2$, so the centered difference cancels the term linear in $h$.

| $h$ | forward | centered |
|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | 3.3100 | 3.0100 |
| 0.01 | 3.0301 | 3.0001 |

Check with more than one increment, and check smoothness first: for $|x|$ at 0 the centered difference is 0 for every $h$, while the one-sided slopes are $-1$ and $+1$. For very small $h$ round-off error from subtracting nearly equal numbers can also spoil the estimate.

sections.title: Worked example: the slope of the sigmoid

parts.md:
$$\sigma'(z)=-(1+e^{-z})^{-2}\cdot(-e^{-z})=\frac{e^{-z}}{(1+e^{-z})^2}.$$

Why: outer $u^{-1}$ gives $-u^{-2}$; the inner function $1+e^{-z}$ has derivative $-e^{-z}$.
parts.title: Apply the chain rule

parts.md:
$$\sigma'(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\cdot\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}=\sigma(z)\bigl(1-\sigma(z)\bigr).$$

Why: $1-\sigma(z)=\dfrac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}$.
parts.title: Factor it

parts.md: With $p=\sigma(z)$: $p(1-p)=\tfrac14-(p-\tfrac12)^2\le\tfrac14$. The maximum $1/4$ occurs at $p=1/2$ (score 0), and the slope tends to 0 as $p$ approaches 0 or 1.
parts.title: Find where it is steepest

parts.md: The same small change in the score changes the probability more near $p=1/2$ than near $p=0$ or $p=1$. At $p=3/4$ the slope is $\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac3{16}$. This factor $p(1-p)$ will reappear in the gradient of the sigmoid loss in Topic 8.
parts.title: Interpret

sections.intro: A formula you will use again in Topic 8.

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
Each solution contains **one** wrong step. Find it first, then open the answer.

**Item 1.** Differentiate $f(x)=\ln(5x)$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 1.** The derivative of $\ln u$ is $1/u$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 2.** With $u=5x$, $f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{5x}$.

:::Which step is wrong?
**Step 1.** The derivative of $\ln u(x)$ is $\dfrac{u'(x)}{u(x)}$: you must multiply by the inner derivative $u'=5$. So $f'(x)=\dfrac{5}{5x}=\dfrac1x$. Check: $\ln(5x)=\ln5+\ln x$, whose derivative is $1/x$.
:::

**Item 2.** Differentiate $f(x)=x\,e^{x}$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 1.** Differentiate each factor: $(x)'=1$ and $(e^x)'=e^x$.

> [!ghi-nho] **Step 2.** Multiply the derivatives: $f'(x)=1\cdot e^x=e^x$.

:::Which step is wrong?
**Step 2.** A product is not differentiated factor by factor: $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$, so $(xe^x)'=1\cdot e^x+x\cdot e^x=e^x+xe^x$. Check at $x=1$: the slope should be $2e\approx5.44$, not $e\approx2.72$.
:::

sections.title: Questions that come up

parts.md: A flat tangent. It is a *candidate* for a minimum or maximum, but not a guarantee: $f(x)=x^3$ has $f'(0)=0$ and keeps rising through 0. Topic 9 returns to this.
parts.title: What does f′(a) = 0 tell me?

parts.md: Use the **product rule** when two functions are *multiplied* ($xe^x$). Use the **chain rule** when one function is *inside* another ($e^{3x}$). A function such as $xe^{3x}$ needs both.
parts.title: Product rule or chain rule?

parts.md: It means the derivative read as an effect: how much the output changes *per additional unit* of the input, for a small change near a given point. It is not a constant unless the function is affine.
parts.title: What does 'marginal' mean?

parts.md: The expansion in $h$ of $f(a+h)$ and $f(a-h)$ contains the same quadratic term with the same sign, so it cancels in $f(a+h)-f(a-h)$. The forward quotient keeps a term proportional to $h$.
parts.title: Why is the centered difference more accurate?

parts.md: If $f$ is differentiable at $a$, then $f(a+h)-f(a)=h\cdot\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$. The quotient tends to $f'(a)$ and $h$ tends to 0, so the product tends to 0: $f(a+h)\to f(a)$, which is continuity.
parts.title: Why does differentiable imply continuous?

sections.title: Practice with Python

parts.md:
`sympy` differentiates symbolically, so you can check your hand calculations; `numpy` checks a derivative numerically. ```html
Python
import sympy as sp

x = sp.symbols("x")
for f in [(3*x + 1)**2, sp.exp(3*x - 1), sp.log(1 + x**2), x*sp.exp(x), sp.log(1 + sp.exp(2*x))]:
    print(f"d/dx [{f}] = {sp.simplify(sp.diff(f, x))}")

g = sp.log(1 + sp.exp(2*x))
print("g'(0) =", sp.diff(g, x).subs(x, 0))
Output
d/dx [(3*x + 1)**2] = 18*x + 6
d/dx [exp(3*x - 1)] = 3*exp(3*x - 1)
d/dx [log(x**2 + 1)] = 2*x/(x**2 + 1)
d/dx [x*exp(x)] = (x + 1)*exp(x)
d/dx [log(exp(2*x) + 1)] = 2*exp(2*x)/(exp(2*x) + 1)
g'(0) = 1
``` ```html
Python
import numpy as np

f = lambda x: x**3
a = 1.0
for h in (0.1, 0.01):
    forward = (f(a + h) - f(a)) / h
    centered = (f(a + h) - f(a - h)) / (2 * h)
    print(f"h = {h}: forward {forward:.4f}, centered {centered:.4f}, exact f'(1) = 3")

# tangent-line estimate of x^2 near 3, and its exact error
estimate = 9 + 6 * 0.02
print("estimate", estimate, " exact", round(3.02**2, 4), " error", round(3.02**2 - estimate, 4))
Output
h = 0.1: forward 3.3100, centered 3.0100, exact f'(1) = 3
h = 0.01: forward 3.0301, centered 3.0001, exact f'(1) = 3
estimate 9.12  exact 9.1204  error 0.0004
``` The first output agrees with the worked examples (for instance $6(3x+1)=18x+6$). In the second, the centered difference is far closer to 3 than the forward difference at the same $h$, and the tangent-line estimate of $f(3.02)$ is low by exactly $0.02^2=0.0004$.

flashcards.title: Flashcards · Derivatives, the chain rule and marginal effects

items.meaning: lim f(x) = L as x → a means f(x) can be made as close to L as we like with x close to a (x ≠ a). The two-sided limit exists iff both one-sided limits agree.
f(a) is defined and lim f(x) = f(a) as x → a.
f′(a) = lim (f(a + h) − f(a))/h as h → 0: the local rate of change and the tangent slope.
Differentiable at a implies continuous at a. The converse fails.
items.example: |x| is continuous at 0, but its quotient is −1 on the left and +1 on the right.

items.meaning: y = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a); for small h, f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)h.
(xᵖ)′ = pxᵖ⁻¹, (fg)′ = f′g + fg′, (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g², (eˣ)′ = eˣ, (ln x)′ = 1/x.
(f∘g)′(x) = f′(g(x))·g′(x): outer derivative at the inner value, times the inner derivative.
A derivative read in context: the change in the output per extra unit of input, for small changes near a point. Δf ≈ f′(a)Δx.
items.example: C′(10) = 7: about 7 more cost per extra unit at q = 10.

items.meaning: f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)h + ½f″(a)h². The second derivative tells how the slope changes.
σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)); the maximum is 1/4 at z = 0 and it vanishes as σ approaches 0 or 1.

summary: A limit describes behaviour near a point; continuity means the value equals the limit; the derivative is the limit of secant slopes.
Differentiable implies continuous, never the other way round: corners like |x| are continuous without a derivative.
Know the basic rules cold; for compositions use the chain rule, one factor per layer, ending with the inner derivative.
A marginal effect is a derivative in context: Δf ≈ f′(a)Δx for small Δx. A rate (slope) and a change are different things.
Second-order terms and centered differences explain how good a tangent-line estimate is; σ′ = σ(1 − σ) is the key derivative for probability models.

quiz.title: Quiz · Derivatives, the chain rule and marginal effects

questions.prompt: What is $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}$?
questions.explanation: For $x\ne3$ the quotient equals $\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}=x+3$, and the limit of $x+3$ as $x\to3$ is 6. The form $0/0$ at $x=3$ is only a signal to simplify; it does not mean the limit is 0 or that it does not exist.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x)=x+2$ for $x\ne 1$ and $f(1)=c$. Which value of $c$ makes $f$ continuous at $1$?
questions.explanation: Continuity requires $f(1)=\lim_{x\to1}f(x)$. Away from 1, $f(x)=x+2$, so the limit is $1+2=3$. Hence $c=3$.

questions.prompt: For $f(x)=x^2$, what is the average rate of change from $x=1$ to $x=3$?
questions.explanation: The secant slope is $\frac{f(3)-f(1)}{3-1}=\frac{9-1}{2}=4$. The value 8 is the total change (not divided by the width 2), and 2 and 6 are the instantaneous slopes $f'(1)$ and $f'(3)$ at the two ends.

questions.prompt: If $f(x)=3x^4-2x$, what is $f'(x)$?
questions.explanation: The power rule gives $(3x^4)'=3\cdot4\,x^3=12x^3$, and the derivative of $-2x$ is $-2$. Options A and D leave out the exponent factor or do not lower the power; option C keeps $x$ in the derivative of a linear term.

questions.prompt: If $f(x)=e^{3x-1}$, what is $f'(x)$?
questions.explanation: The outer function $e^u$ has derivative $e^u$, and the inner function $3x-1$ has derivative 3. The chain rule multiplies them: $f'(x)=3e^{3x-1}$. Option D forgets the inner factor; option B treats $e^u$ as if it were a power $u^n$.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes $f(x)=|x|$ at $x=0$?
questions.explanation: Both one-sided limits at 0 equal 0, which equals $f(0)$, so $f$ is continuous. The difference quotient $|h|/h$ is $-1$ on the left and $1$ on the right, so $f'(0)$ does not exist: the graph has a corner.

options.label: It is discontinuous and fails to be differentiable.
It is continuous and fails to be differentiable.

questions.prompt: For $x\lt1$, let $f(x)=ax+b$. For $x\ge1$, let $f(x)=x^2+2$. Which pair $(a,b)$ makes $f$ differentiable at $x=1$?
questions.explanation: Differentiability needs continuity and equal slopes at the join. Values: $a+b=1^2+2=3$. Slopes: the left slope is $a$ and the right slope is $2x=2$ at $x=1$, so $a=2$. Then $b=1$. Options A and B match the values but not the slopes; option C matches the slope but not the values.

questions.prompt: Total cost is $C(q)=50+2q+0.2q^2$. What increase in cost does the first-order approximation at $q=5$ predict when output rises by $0.25$?
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is $C'(q)=2+0.4q$, so $C'(5)=4$ (money per unit). The first-order estimate of the change is $4\cdot0.25=1$. The exact change, $1.0125$, adds the quadratic term $0.2(0.25)^2=0.0125$ that the linear approximation omits. Option B is the rate itself, not a change; option A uses $C'(5)=3$ because it differentiates $0.2q^2$ as $0.2q$.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x)=\ln(2+e^{3x})$. What is $f'\!\left(\dfrac{\ln 4}{3}\right)$?
questions.explanation: By the chain rule $f'(x)=\dfrac{3e^{3x}}{2+e^{3x}}$: the outer $\ln u$ gives $1/u$ and the inner $u=2+e^{3x}$ gives $3e^{3x}$. At $x=(\ln4)/3$ we have $e^{3x}=4$, so $f'=\frac{12}{6}=2$. Option C forgets the inner factor 3 (giving $4/6$); option D forgets the factor $1/u$ (giving $3\cdot4=12$).

questions.prompt: Use the second-order Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ at $x=4$ to approximate $f(4.4)$. What value does the polynomial give?
questions.explanation: At 4: $f=2$, $f'=\frac1{2\sqrt x}=\frac14$ and $f''=-\frac14x^{-3/2}=-\frac1{32}$. With $h=0.4$ the polynomial is $2+\frac h4-\frac{h^2}{64}=2+0.1-0.0025=2.0975$. (The exact value is about $2.09762$.) Option B stops at the tangent line; option C drops the factor $\tfrac12$ of the curvature term; option A has the wrong sign for it.

questions.prompt: For $f(x)=x^3$, what is the centered difference $\dfrac{f(2+h)-f(2-h)}{2h}$ at $h=0.2$?
questions.explanation: Expanding the two cubes gives $(2+h)^3-(2-h)^3=24h+2h^3$, so the quotient is $12+h^2=12.04$ at $h=0.2$. The forward difference is $13.24$ and the backward difference $10.84$. The exact derivative is $f'(2)=12$, which is not what any finite-$h$ difference returns; the centered difference only cancels the term of order $h$, leaving the error $h^2$.

questions.prompt: Let $p(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$ and $\ell(z)=\tfrac12\bigl(p(z)-1\bigr)^2$. What is $\ell''(\ln 3)$?
questions.explanation: At $z=\ln3$: $p=3/4$, $p'=p(1-p)=3/16$ and $p''=p'(1-2p)=-3/32$. Differentiating $\ell'=(p-1)p'$ with the product rule gives $\ell''=(p')^2+(p-1)p''=\frac{9}{256}+\frac{6}{256}=\frac{15}{256}$. Option B keeps only $(p')^2$, as if $(fg)'=f'g'$.

questions.prompt:
Let
$f(x)=\begin{cases}2x^2,&x\lt 0,\\ x^3,&x\ge 0.\end{cases}$
Which statement holds near or at $x=0$?
questions.explanation: The difference quotients of $f$ tend to 0 from both sides, so $f'(0)=0$. The formulas $4x$ (left) and $3x^2$ (right) both tend to 0, so $f'$ is continuous. But the difference quotients of $f'$ tend to $4$ from the left and $0$ from the right, so the second derivative fails to exist at the join.

options.label: $f$ is continuously differentiable near $0$, and $f''(0)$ does not exist.
$f$ is twice continuously differentiable near $0$, with $f''(0)=0$.
$f$ is continuous near $0$, and $f'(0)$ does not exist.
$f$ is twice continuously differentiable near $0$, with $f''(0)=4$.

questions.prompt: For a polynomial $f$ of degree at most 3, let $C_h=\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a-h)}{2h}$, with $h\gt 0$. Which expression always equals $f'(a)$ exactly?
questions.explanation: For a cubic, expanding exactly gives $C_h=f'(a)+ch^2$ with $c=f'''(a)/6$. Replacing $h$ by $h/2$ divides the error by 4, so $4C_{h/2}-C_h=4f'(a)+ch^2-f'(a)-ch^2=3f'(a)$, and dividing by 3 gives $f'(a)$ exactly. This is a simple instance of Richardson extrapolation.

questions.prompt: What is $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(5x)$ for $x\gt 0$?
questions.explanation: By the chain rule $\frac{d}{dx}\ln u=\frac{u'}{u}=\frac{5}{5x}=\frac1x$. Equivalently $\ln(5x)=\ln5+\ln x$ and the constant $\ln5$ disappears. Writing $1/(5x)$ forgets the inner derivative, $5x$ confuses $\ln$ with its derivative, and $5/x$ wrongly treats $\ln(5x)$ as $5\ln x$.

questions.prompt: If $f$ is continuous at $a$, then $f$ is differentiable at $a$.
questions.explanation: False. Differentiable implies continuous, but not the other way round. $f(x)=|x|$ is continuous at 0 and has a corner there: the difference quotient is $-1$ from the left and $+1$ from the right.

questions.prompt: Match each function with its derivative.
questions.explanation: The first three are chain rule (outer derivative times inner derivative: $e^{2x}\cdot2$, $2(3x+1)\cdot3$, $\frac{1}{3x+1}\cdot3$). $xe^x$ needs the product rule. The last is $\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)$ from the worked example.

questions.prompt: Use the tangent line to $f(x)=x^2$ at $a=3$ to estimate $f(3.02)$. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: $f(3)=9$ and $f'(3)=6$, so $f(3.02)\approx9+6(0.02)=9.12$. The exact value is $9.1204$; the estimate is low by $0.0004=(0.02)^2$.

questions.prompt: For one observation $x=2$, $y=3$ with $b=0$ and $w=1$, the squared error is $\ell(w)=(b+wx-y)^2$. What is $\ell'(1)$? Enter a number.
questions.explanation: By the chain rule $\ell'(w)=2(b+wx-y)\,x$. At $w=1$: $r=2-3=-1$, so $\ell'(1)=2(-1)(2)=-4$. The negative sign says that raising $w$ lowers the loss.

lessons.title: Topic 8 · Partial Derivatives and the Gradient
lessons.description: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, the gradient and its meaning as the direction of steepest increase, and the gradients of squared-error and sigmoid losses.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
objectives: Compute partial derivatives of functions of two or three variables and assemble the gradient
Evaluate a directional derivative with a unit vector and explain why the gradient is the steepest-ascent direction
Use the linear approximation F(a + h) ≈ F(a) + ∇F(a)·h to estimate changes
Derive and evaluate the gradient of MSE and half-MSE for a line, and of a sigmoid loss, with the chain rule
Apply the chain rule along a path and say what 'per unit of t' versus 'per unit distance' means
Decide when the formula D_uF = ∇F · u applies, and when only the existence of partials is known
lessons.body:
A real model has many parameters, not one. A line has $(b,w)$, a regression with ten features has eleven numbers, and a neural network has millions. To train it we need to know how the loss responds to **each** parameter and, just as important, in which **direction** to move all of them at once. Partial derivatives answer the first question and the **gradient** answers the second.

> [!ghi-nho] A function of several variables $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ gives one number for each vector $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$. Its **partial derivative** $\partial F/\partial x_j$ is the ordinary derivative along the slice where only $x_j$ moves. The **gradient** $\nabla F$ stacks all $n$ partial derivatives into one column vector.

:::Predict before you compute
Let $F(b,w)=b^2+3bw+2w^2$ and stand at $(b,w)=(1,2)$. If you increase $b$ by a tiny amount, does $F$ rise faster than if you increase $w$ by the same amount? And if you could move in any direction, roughly how fast could $F$ increase per unit distance? Make a guess (a number is fine) and compare with the examples below.
:::

sections.title: Partial derivatives are slopes of slices

parts.md: For $F(b,w)=b^2+3bw+2w^2$ the graph is the surface $z=F(b,w)$ over the $(b,w)$-plane. Fix $w$ at a number and you get an ordinary curve in $b$; fix $b$ and you get a different curve in $w$.
parts.title: Slicing a surface

parts.md:
$$\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_j}(a)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{F(a+t\,e_j)-F(a)}{t},$$

where $e_j$ has a 1 in coordinate $j$ and 0 elsewhere. All other coordinates stay at their current values.
parts.title: Definition

parts.md: Treat every other variable as a **constant** and use the one-variable rules you already know. The product $3bw$ contributes $3w$ when $b$ varies and $3b$ when $w$ varies.
parts.title: In practice

sections.title: Worked example: two partial derivatives

parts.md:
Hold $w$ fixed, so $w$ is a constant:

$$\frac{\partial F}{\partial b}=2b+3w .$$

Why: $b^2\to2b$; $3bw=(3w)\,b\to3w$; $2w^2$ is a constant, so $\to0$.
parts.title: Differentiate with respect to b

parts.md:
Hold $b$ fixed:

$$\frac{\partial F}{\partial w}=3b+4w .$$

Why: $b^2\to0$; $3bw=(3b)\,w\to3b$; $2w^2\to4w$.
parts.title: Differentiate with respect to w

parts.md:
$$\frac{\partial F}{\partial b}(1,2)=2+6=8,\qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial w}(1,2)=3+8=11 .$$

Why: substitute the point only **after** differentiating.
parts.title: Evaluate at (1, 2)
