Why: independence removes the covariance terms, and the factor $1/n$ outside the sum is squared.
parts.title: Its variance (independence)

parts.md:
$$\text{SE}(\bar X)=\sqrt{V(\bar X)}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$$

Why: the standard error of an estimator is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution.
parts.title: Standard error

parts.md: Nothing here required the population to be normal. The mean and the standard error hold for **any** population with a finite variance; only the *shape* of the sampling distribution depends on the population.
parts.title: What was not assumed

sections.intro: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be an iid sample (independent, identically distributed) from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2<\infty$, and let $\bar X=\frac1n\sum_iX_i$.

sections.title: Worked example: standard error and sample size

parts.md:
$$\text{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=\frac{12}6=2$$

Why: the answer is not 12; that is the spread of single observations.
parts.title: Apply the formula

parts.md:
$$n=144:\quad\text{SE}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{144}}=\frac{12}{12}=1$$

Why: replacing $n$ by $4n$ multiplies the standard error by $1/\sqrt4=\tfrac12$.
parts.title: Quadruple the sample size

parts.md:
To reach $\text{SE}=0.5$ we need $\sqrt n=12/0.5=24$, so $n=576$.

| $n$ | 9 | 36 | 144 | 576 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{SE}=12/\sqrt n$ | 4 | 2 | 1 | 0.5 |

Why: precision has diminishing returns: halving the error costs four times the data.
parts.title: How many observations for a given precision?

sections.intro: A population has $\sigma=12$. Find the standard error of the sample mean for $n=36$, and see what happens when the sample size changes.

sections.title: Worked example: an exponential population

parts.md:
$$n=5:\ V(\bar X)=\tfrac{100}5=20;\qquad n=25:\ V(\bar X)=\tfrac{100}{25}=4,\ \text{SE}=2$$

Why: the centre stays at 10 in both cases, and the spread decreases. These identities are exact.
parts.title: Moments of the sample mean

parts.md:
$$P(\bar X\le12)\approx\Phi\Big(\frac{12-10}2\Big)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\quad(n=25)$$

Why: the central limit theorem says $(\bar X-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ is approximately $N(0,1)$. This step is an **approximation**.
parts.title: Standardize and apply the CLT

parts.md:
For exponential data $\bar X$ follows a Gamma distribution, so the exact value can be computed. It is $0.8428$ for $n=25$ but $0.7149$ for $n=5$, where the normal approximation gives $0.6726$.

Why: the approximation is good at $n=25$ and poor at $n=5$, because the population is skewed. “Large enough” depends on the population shape.
parts.title: Compare with the exact value

sections.intro: Observations are exponential with scale $\beta=10$, so $\mu=10$ and $\sigma^2=100$. What happens to the mean of $n=5$ and of $n=25$ observations?

sections.title: The central limit theorem

parts.md:
> [!ghi-nho] **Central limit theorem.** Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be iid with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $0\lt\sigma^2\lt\infty$. As $n\to\infty$,

$$\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\;\xrightarrow{\ d\ }\;N(0,1)$$

The arrow means convergence in distribution: for large $n$ probabilities about the standardized mean can be approximated with the standard normal CDF $\Phi$.

Three points matter for using it:

- If the observations are **themselves normal**, then $\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$ **exactly** for every $n$. For other populations the CLT gives an approximation.
- The theorem is about the **centred and scaled average**. It does **not** make the original observations normal, and standardizing a non-normal variable does not make it normal.
- It does not give a universal cut-off for “large” $n$. How good the approximation is depends on the population shape and on the probability you are computing; the more skewed the population, the larger the $n$ needed.

sections.title: Worked example: probabilities for a sample mean

parts.md: $$E(\bar X)=50,\qquad \text{SE}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=2,\qquad \bar X\approx N(50,\,2^2)$$
parts.title: The sampling distribution

parts.md:
$$P(47\le\bar X\le53)=\Phi(1.5)-\Phi(-1.5)=2(0.9332)-1\approx0.8664$$

Why: about 87% of sample means fall within 3 units (1.5 standard errors) of 50.
parts.title: An interval

parts.md:
$$P(\bar X\gt53\mid\bar X\gt50)=\frac{P(\bar X\gt53)}{P(\bar X\gt50)}\approx\frac{0.0668}{0.5}=0.1336$$

Why: the event $\{\bar X\gt53\}$ is contained in $\{\bar X\gt50\}$, so the intersection is the smaller event. Divide by the probability of the conditioning event.
parts.title: A conditional probability

sections.intro: A population has mean $\mu=50$ and standard deviation $\sigma=12$. A sample of $n=36$ is drawn. Use the normal approximation for $\bar X$.

sections.title: Law of large numbers versus central limit theorem

parts.md:
$\bar X\xrightarrow{P}\mu$: the sample mean **concentrates** around the true mean as $n$ grows.

It is a statement about where $\bar X$ ends up. We saw the reason: $V(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n\to0$.
parts.title: Law of large numbers (LLN)

parts.md:
$\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$: the **shape** of the standardized error becomes normal.

It is a statement about the distribution of the error. It tells you how large the error of $\bar X$ is likely to be at a given $n$.
parts.title: Central limit theorem (CLT)

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] The two results are complementary: concentration around the truth (LLN) and the shape of the scaled error (CLT).

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
**Solution A.** “The population has $\sigma=12$. A sample of 36 observations has mean $\bar x=50$. So the typical error of $\bar x$ is $\text{SE}=\sigma=12$.”

**Solution B.** “By the central limit theorem, for $n=100$ the individual observations are approximately normal, so I can use the normal table for a single observation.”

:::Where is the error in Solution A?
The standard error of the mean is $\sigma/\sqrt n=12/6=2$. The value 12 is the spread of single observations. Quoting 12 overstates the uncertainty of the sample mean by a factor of $\sqrt n=6$.
:::

:::Where is the error in Solution B?
The CLT is about the distribution of the **sample mean**, not of the individual observations; those keep the population's distribution however large $n$ is. The normal table can be used for $\bar X$ (approximately), but not for one observation from a skewed population.
:::

sections.title: Common questions

parts.md: There is no universal answer. The common cut-off of $n\ge30$ is a rule of thumb. For the exponential population above $n=25$ is already good for $P(\bar X\le12)$ but $n=5$ is not, and for very skewed populations you need far more.
parts.title: How large must n be for the CLT to work?

parts.md: Yes. A sum $S_n=n\bar X$ has mean $n\mu$ and variance $n\sigma^2$, and $(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ is the same standardized quantity as for $\bar X$.
parts.title: Does the CLT apply to sums as well as means?

parts.md: Estimate it with the sample standard deviation $s$ and use the estimated standard error $s/\sqrt n$. For a normal population this changes the standard normal to a $t$ distribution (Topic 15).
parts.title: What if σ is unknown?

parts.md: No. The population distribution and its standard deviation $\sigma$ stay the same. A bigger sample only makes the *sample mean* more precise.
parts.title: Does a bigger sample change the distribution of the observations?

parts.md: The theoretical standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ is a property of the model and the sample size. In practice $\sigma$ is unknown, so we report the estimated standard error from the data.
parts.title: Is the standard error a property of my data?

sections.title: Practice with Python

parts.md:
A simulation is the most direct way to see a sampling distribution. We draw 20,000 repeated samples from the exponential population, compute the mean of each, and compare with theory. The seed is fixed so the numbers are reproducible. Notice the standard deviation of $\bar X$ falling like $10/\sqrt n$ and the skewness decreasing toward 0 (the normal value). ```html 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)
beta = 10                                   # exponential population: mean 10, sd 10
print("  n  mean(Xbar)  sd(Xbar)  theory SE  skewness  P(Xbar<=12)  CLT approx")
for n in (1, 5, 25, 100):
    xbar = rng.exponential(beta, size=(20_000, n)).mean(axis=1)   # 20,000 repeated samples
    se = beta / np.sqrt(n)
    print(f"{n:3d}  {xbar.mean():9.3f}  {xbar.std():8.3f}  {se:9.3f}  {stats.skew(xbar):8.3f}  "
          f"{np.mean(xbar <= 12):11.4f}  {stats.norm.cdf((12 - 10) / se):10.4f}")

Output

  n  mean(Xbar)  sd(Xbar)  theory SE  skewness  P(Xbar<=12)  CLT approx
  1      9.984     9.940     10.000     1.958       0.6978      0.5793
  5     10.007     4.509      4.472     0.922       0.7123      0.6726
 25     10.006     2.007      2.000     0.404       0.8425      0.8413
100     10.001     1.009      1.000     0.203       0.9706      0.9772
``` The exact distribution of the mean of exponential variables is Gamma, which lets us check the CLT approximation, and the standard error table is easy to reproduce: ```html 
from scipy import stats

# Exact: the mean of n exponential(scale=10) values is Gamma(shape=n, scale=10/n)
for n in (5, 25):
    exact = stats.gamma(n, scale=10 / n).cdf(12)
    approx = stats.norm.cdf((12 - 10) / (10 / n ** 0.5))
    print(f"n={n:2d}: exact P(Xbar<=12) = {exact:.4f}   CLT approximation = {approx:.4f}")

sigma = 12
for n in (36, 144, 576):
    print(f"sigma={sigma}, n={n:3d}: SE = {sigma / n ** 0.5}")

Output

n= 5: exact P(Xbar<=12) = 0.7149   CLT approximation = 0.6726
n=25: exact P(Xbar<=12) = 0.8428   CLT approximation = 0.8413
sigma=12, n= 36: SE = 2.0
sigma=12, n=144: SE = 1.0
sigma=12, n=576: SE = 0.5
```

flashcards.title: Flashcards · Sampling Distributions and the CLT

items.meaning: A function of the sample that does not involve unknown parameters; it is random before the data are observed.
The distribution of a statistic over repeated samples of the same size from the same model.
X1, …, Xn independent and drawn from the same distribution.
E(X̄) = μ for any iid sample with finite mean.
V(X̄) = σ²/n for an iid sample with variance σ².
SE(X̄) = σ/√n, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution; quadrupling n halves it.
(X̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) converges in distribution to N(0, 1); the observations need not be normal.
If the observations are N(μ, σ²), then X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) exactly for every n.
X̄ converges to μ in probability: the mean concentrates; the CLT describes the shape of the scaled error.

summary: A statistic such as X̄ is random before the data are seen; its sampling distribution describes its values over repeated samples, and it is not the histogram of one sample.
For an iid sample, E(X̄) = μ and V(X̄) = σ²/n, so SE(X̄) = σ/√n; none of this needs normality.
Individual spread σ and the standard error σ/√n are different quantities; quadrupling n halves the standard error.
The CLT says the standardized sample mean is approximately N(0, 1) for large n, for any population with finite variance; the quality depends on the population shape.
If the population is normal, X̄ is exactly normal for every n.
The law of large numbers (X̄ concentrates at μ) and the CLT (the scaled error is approximately normal) answer different questions.

quiz.title: Check your understanding · Sampling Distributions and the CLT

questions.prompt: An iid sample of size $n=36$ comes from a population with standard deviation $\sigma=12$. What is $\text{SE}(\bar X)$?
questions.explanation: The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n=12/6=2$, not the individual-observation spread 12.

questions.prompt: Before an iid sample is observed, which quantity is random in a model with fixed population parameters?
questions.explanation: The sample mean is a statistic and varies across repeated samples. The population parameters are fixed, although they may be unknown.

questions.prompt: Under the same iid sampling model, the sample size increases from $n$ to $4n$. What happens to the theoretical standard error of $\bar X$?
questions.explanation: Because $\text{SE}(\bar X)=\sigma/\sqrt n$, replacing $n$ by $4n$ multiplies the standard error by $1/\sqrt4=1/2$. The standard error falls like $1/\sqrt n$, not like $1/n$.

questions.prompt: For iid observations with finite mean and finite, positive variance, which statement correctly distinguishes the law of large numbers (LLN) from the central limit theorem (CLT)?
questions.explanation: The LLN states $\bar X\xrightarrow{P}\mu$. The CLT states $\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$. Concentration of the mean and the shape of its scaled error are different conclusions.

options.label: The LLN makes the individual observations normal; the CLT makes their variance zero.
The CLT makes $\bar X$ exactly normal for every sample size, even for a nonnormal population.
The LLN states that the standardized error converges to zero; the CLT says that $\bar X$ does not concentrate.
The LLN concerns convergence of $\bar X$ to $\mu$; the CLT concerns the distribution of the standardized error.

questions.prompt: Let $X_1,\dots,X_{100}$ be iid exponential variables with scale $\beta=10$. Use the CLT normal approximation and $\Phi(1)\approx0.8413$ to approximate $P(\bar X\gt11\mid\bar X\gt10)$.
questions.explanation: The sample mean has mean 10 and standard error $10/\sqrt{100}=1$. Under the normal approximation, $P(\bar X\gt11)\approx0.1587$ and $P(\bar X\gt10)\approx0.5$. The first event is contained in the second, so the conditional probability is approximately $0.1587/0.5=0.3174$.

questions.prompt: A population has $\sigma=20$. Find the standard error of the mean of $n=100$ observations.
questions.explanation: $\text{SE}=\sigma/\sqrt n=20/10=2$.

questions.prompt: The population standard deviation is $\sigma=10$. How many observations $n$ are needed for the standard error of the sample mean to equal 1?
questions.explanation: $\sigma/\sqrt n=1\Rightarrow\sqrt n=10\Rightarrow n=100$.

questions.prompt: If the population distribution is normal, then $\bar X$ is exactly normally distributed for every sample size $n\ge1$.
questions.explanation: True. A sum of independent normal variables is normal, so $\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$ exactly, whatever $n$ is. The CLT is needed only for non-normal populations.

questions.prompt: The sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is the distribution of the $n$ values in the one sample you collected.
questions.explanation: False. The $n$ values in one sample are one realization of the data. The sampling distribution describes the values $\bar X$ would take over repeated samples of size $n$ from the same model.

questions.prompt: A population has $\mu=50$ and $\sigma=12$. Use the CLT with $n=36$ and $\Phi(2)\approx0.9772$ to approximate $P(\bar X\gt54)$.

lessons.title: Topic 15 · Statistical Estimation and Confidence Intervals
lessons.description: Parameters, statistics, estimators and estimates; bias and MSE; confidence intervals for a proportion and a mean; efficiency, consistency, the method of moments and maximum likelihood.
objectives: Distinguish a parameter, a statistic, an estimator and an estimate
Compute the bias and mean squared error of an estimator and compare two estimators
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for a proportion and for a normal mean
Explain what a confidence level does and does not mean in terms of repeated sampling
Compare estimators by relative efficiency and explain consistency
Derive the method-of-moments and maximum-likelihood estimates for the Bernoulli, uniform and normal models
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson you can:
lessons.body:
Statistics reverses the question of probability. In probability, the model is given and we ask what data it might produce. In **estimation**, the data are given and we ask what they tell us about the model. A fraction of 40 out of 200 visitors completed an action: what is the population probability $p$, and how sure can we be? This lesson turns the sampling distributions of Topic 14 into tools: **estimators** and their properties (bias, variance, mean squared error, efficiency, consistency), **confidence intervals** that attach uncertainty to an estimate, and two ways of constructing estimators: the **method of moments** and **maximum likelihood**. Maximum likelihood is the principle behind logistic regression and most training objectives in machine learning.

> [!ghi-nho] The lecture follows one chain: model and assumptions $\rightarrow$ sampling distribution $\rightarrow$ estimator $\rightarrow$ uncertainty. Always report the estimate, its uncertainty, and the assumptions behind both.

**Predict first.** A 95% confidence interval for the action probability is $[0.145,\,0.255]$. Is it correct to say: "there is a 95% probability that $p$ lies between 0.145 and 0.255"? Decide, and then open the box.

:::Check your prediction
Not in the frequentist interpretation used in this course. The parameter $p$ is a fixed number, so it either is in this particular interval or it is not. The 95% describes the **procedure**: if you repeated the sampling many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain $p$. The long-run interpretation is explored in the worked example and the simulation below.
:::

sections.title: Parameters, statistics, estimators and estimates

parts.md:
Four words that sound alike but mean different things. Using the website data ($k=40$ successes among $n=200$ visitors):

| Term | Meaning | Website example |
|---|---|---|
| **Parameter** | A fixed characteristic of the population model (fixed does not mean known) | $p$, the population action probability |
| **Statistic** | A function of the sample not involving unknown parameters | $K=\sum_iX_i$, the number of successes |
| **Estimator** | A statistic used to estimate a parameter; random before sampling | $\hat p=K/n$ |
| **Estimate** | The numerical value of the estimator for the recorded sample | $40/200=0.20$ |

Familiar estimators for an iid sample are

$$\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2,\qquad \hat p=\frac Kn=\bar X\ \ (\text{0/1 data})$$

They estimate $\mu$, $\sigma^2$ and $p$. The estimator varies across repeated samples; one estimate is just a number and does not by itself say how good the rule is.

> [!canh-bao] Do not confuse the sample standard deviation $S$ (spread of the data) with the estimated standard error $S/\sqrt n$ (uncertainty of the mean).

sections.title: Worked example: bias and mean squared error

parts.md:
$0.03\lt0.04$, so the **biased** estimator B has the smaller mean squared error.

Why: B's reduction in variance outweighs its squared bias. Unbiasedness concerns only the centre of the sampling distribution; precision also depends on the spread.
parts.title: Compare

parts.md:
Let $\hat\mu=\bar X+1/n$. Then $B=1/n$ and adding a constant leaves the variance at $\sigma^2/n$:

$$\text{MSE}(\hat\mu)=\frac{\sigma^2}n+\frac1{n^2}$$

Why: the bias enters **squared**. As $n$ grows both terms vanish.
parts.title: Shifted sample mean

parts.md:
Write $\hat\theta-\theta=[\hat\theta-E(\hat\theta)]+[E(\hat\theta)-\theta]$, square and take expectations. The cross term has mean zero because $E[\hat\theta-E(\hat\theta)]=0$.

Why: this is the same split of $E[(X-c)^2]$ into variance plus squared offset from Topic 12.
parts.title: Where the decomposition comes from

sections.intro: The bias of $\hat\theta$ is $B(\hat\theta)=E(\hat\theta)-\theta$, and $\text{MSE}(\hat\theta)=E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]=V(\hat\theta)+[B(\hat\theta)]^2$. Compare two estimators of the same parameter.

sections.title: Worked example: a confidence interval for a proportion

parts.md:
$$\hat p=\frac{40}{200}=0.20,\qquad \widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}n}=\sqrt{\frac{0.20(0.80)}{200}}\approx0.02828$$

Why: $V(\hat p)=p(1-p)/n$, and the unknown $p$ is replaced by $\hat p$.
parts.title: Estimate and standard error

parts.md:
$$z_{0.025}\approx1.96\;\Rightarrow\;1.96(0.02828)\approx0.0554$$

Why: $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the upper-tail critical value with $P(Z\gt z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$.
parts.title: Margin of error

parts.md:
$$\hat p\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}n}=0.20\pm0.0554=[0.145,\ 0.255]$$

Why: an approximate statement about the **population probability** $p$, not a range for individual visitors.
parts.title: The interval

parts.md:
With 160 successes in 800 trials, $\hat p$ is still $0.20$ but $\widehat{\text{SE}}\approx0.01414$ and the interval is $[0.172,\ 0.228]$.

Why: the margin of error halves (0.0277 against 0.0554) because $n$ is four times as large.
parts.title: Quadruple the sample

parts.md: The interval relies on independent trials with a common $p$ and a normal approximation. It is not exact, especially with few successes or failures; with all failures the plug-in standard error is zero, which does **not** mean $p$ is known exactly.
parts.title: Check the assumptions

sections.intro: Among 200 iid Bernoulli responses, 40 are successes. Build an approximate 95% interval for $p$, then see the effect of a larger sample.

sections.title: Worked example: a confidence interval for a mean

parts.md:
$$T=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}$$

Why: because $\sigma$ is replaced by $S$, the standardized mean has a Student $t$ distribution with $n-1=15$ degrees of freedom. It has heavier tails than the standard normal.
parts.title: Pivot

parts.md: $$\widehat{\text{SE}}=\frac s{\sqrt n}=\frac4{\sqrt{16}}=1$$
parts.title: Estimated standard error

parts.md: For normal data this interval is exact for any $n\ge2$; it is not only for small samples. With 1.96 instead of 2.131 the interval would be too narrow, and its coverage would fall below 95% (the simulation below gives about 93% at $n=16$).
parts.title: What changes with the assumptions

sections.intro: An iid sample of $n=16$ from a **normal** population with unknown variance gives $\bar x=10$ and $s=4$. Use $t_{0.025,15}\approx2.131$.

sections.title: What 95% confidence does and does not mean

parts.md:
- Approximately 95% of intervals built by this procedure, over repeated samples, contain the fixed true parameter.
- The level describes the **long-run coverage of the procedure**.
- A larger confidence level (99%) uses a larger critical value and gives a wider interval; a larger $n$ gives a narrower one.
parts.title: Correct readings

parts.md:
- "There is a 95% probability that $p$ is in this interval." The parameter is fixed; the realized interval either contains it or not.
- "95% of the observations lie in the interval." It is an interval for $p$ or $\mu$, not for individual outcomes.
- "Exactly 19 of any 20 intervals contain the parameter." It is only 95% on average over many repetitions.
parts.title: Incorrect readings

sections.outro: > [!canh-bao] A confidence interval for a mean or proportion is not an interval containing 95% of the individual observations, and it is not a probability distribution for the parameter. Approximate procedures, like the proportion interval above, have coverage only approximately equal to the stated level, and only under their assumptions.

sections.title: Worked example: efficiency and consistency

parts.md:
Suppose $V(\hat\theta_1)=0.5$ and $V(\hat\theta_2)=2$:

$$\text{eff}(\hat\theta_1,\hat\theta_2)=\frac{2}{0.5}=4$$

Why: a value greater than 1 favours $\hat\theta_1$, because it has the smaller variance.
parts.title: Compute the ratio

parts.md:
For independent unbiased $T_1,T_2$ with variances $1$ and $3$, take $T_w=wT_1+(1-w)T_2$, which is unbiased for any $w$:

$$V(T_w)=w^2(1)+(1-w)^2(3)$$

Why: independence kills the covariance, and the weights are squared in the variance.
parts.title: Combine the two estimators

parts.md:
$$\frac d{dw}V(T_w)=2w-6(1-w)=0\;\Rightarrow\;w=\frac34,\qquad V(T_w)=\frac9{16}+\frac3{16}=\frac34$$

Why: the more precise $T_1$ gets the larger weight, and the combined variance $3/4$ is below both $1$ and $3$.
parts.title: Minimize

parts.md:
$\hat\theta_n$ is **consistent** if $P(|\hat\theta_n-\theta|\gt\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon\gt0$.

An unbiased estimator with variance $4/n$ is consistent: its variance tends to 0 as $n\to\infty$, so large errors become increasingly unlikely. This is how $\bar X$ is consistent for $\mu$ (the law of large numbers).

Why: unbiasedness at a fixed $n$ and consistency as $n$ grows are different properties.
parts.title: Consistency

sections.intro: For two unbiased estimators of the same parameter, the efficiency of $\hat\theta_1$ relative to $\hat\theta_2$ is $\text{eff}(\hat\theta_1,\hat\theta_2)=V(\hat\theta_2)/V(\hat\theta_1)$.

sections.title: Worked example: the method of moments

parts.md:
$E(X)=p$, so match $p=\bar X$:

$$\hat p_{\text{MM}}=\bar X=K/n$$

For $k=3$, $n=10$ this gives $0.3$.
parts.title: Bernoulli

parts.md:
$E(X)=\theta/2$. Suppose the observed values are $3,5,10$, so $\bar x=6$:

$$\frac{\hat\theta}2=6\;\Rightarrow\;\hat\theta_{\text{MM}}=2\bar x=12$$

Why: set the **population moment** (not $\theta$) equal to the sample moment. Setting $\theta=\bar x$ would be a mistake.
parts.title: Uniform(0, θ)

parts.md:
The estimate $12$ is at least as large as the largest observation $10$, as it must be for this model. A moment estimate need not respect that in general (a small sample could give $2\bar x\lt\max_i x_i$), so always check the solution.

Why: moment matching builds an estimator; it does not guarantee unbiasedness or efficiency.
parts.title: Check against the parameter space

sections.intro: Match population moments (functions of the parameter) to sample moments, and solve for the parameter: $\mu_r'(\hat\theta)=m_r'=\frac1n\sum_iX_i^r$.

sections.title: Worked example: maximum likelihood

parts.md:
For $k$ successes in $n$ trials,

$$L(p)=p^k(1-p)^{n-k},\qquad \ell(p)=k\log p+(n-k)\log(1-p)$$

Why: the logarithm is increasing, so it keeps the maximizer and turns a product into a sum.
parts.title: Bernoulli likelihood

parts.md:
$$\ell'(p)=\frac kp-\frac{n-k}{1-p}=0\;\Rightarrow\;k(1-p)=(n-k)p\;\Rightarrow\;\hat p_{\text{MLE}}=\frac kn$$

For $k=3$, $n=10$ the log-likelihood is $3\log p+7\log(1-p)$ with maximum at $0.3$. The second derivative $-k/p^2-(n-k)/(1-p)^2$ is negative, confirming a maximum.
parts.title: Maximize

parts.md:
For iid $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with both unknown, the MLEs are

$$\hat\mu=\bar X,\qquad \hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2$$

For the data $1,3,8$: $\bar x=4$, centred sum of squares $9+1+16=26$, so $\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}=26/3\approx8.67$, while $s^2=26/2=13$.
parts.title: Normal model

parts.md:
$$E(\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}})=\frac{n-1}n\sigma^2,\qquad E(S^2)=\sigma^2$$

Why: the MLE is biased downward; dividing by $n-1$ removes the bias. The method says how an estimator is constructed, the property says how it behaves over repeated samples.
parts.title: The MLE is biased here

parts.md:
$L(\theta)=\theta^{-n}$ for $\theta\ge\max_ix_i$ and $0$ otherwise. It decreases in $\theta$ on its support, so the maximum is at the **largest observation**: for $3,5,10$, $\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=10$ while $\hat\theta_{\text{MM}}=12$.

Why: the two methods need not agree. They agree for the Bernoulli, but that is specific to that example.
parts.title: Uniform(0, θ)

sections.intro: The likelihood is the probability (or density) of the observed sample viewed as a function of the parameter, $L(\theta)=\prod_if(x_i\mid\theta)$. The MLE maximizes it. The data are fixed and the parameter varies.

sections.title: Sufficiency: what a summary retains

parts.md:
For iid Bernoulli data, any sequence with $k$ successes has probability

$$P(X_1=x_1,\dots,X_n=x_n)=p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$$
parts.title: Probability of one arrangement

parts.md:
$$P(X_1=x_1,\dots,X_n=x_n\mid K=k)=\frac{p^k(1-p)^{n-k}}{\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}}=\frac1{\binom nk}$$

Why: the answer no longer contains $p$. For $n=5$, $k=2$, every one of the $10$ arrangements has conditional probability $1/10$.
parts.title: Condition on the count

parts.md: Once you know the number of successes (and $n$), the order in which they occurred carries no extra information about $p$. Sufficiency is defined relative to a model and a parameter; it does not say that the summary preserves every feature of the data.
parts.title: Interpretation

sections.intro: A statistic is **sufficient** for a parameter if the conditional distribution of the whole sample given that statistic does not depend on the parameter.

sections.title: Find the error in the solution

parts.md:
**Solution A.** For the data $x=2,4,6,8$ a student computes the sample variance: “$\bar x=5$, and $\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=9+1+1+9=20$, so $s^2=20/4=5$.”

**Solution B.** “The 95% interval for $p$ is $[0.145,0.255]$, so there is a 95% probability that $p$ is between these values.”

:::Where is the error in Solution A?
The unbiased sample variance divides by $n-1=3$, not by $n=4$: $s^2=20/3\approx6.67$. Dividing by $n$ gives the maximum-likelihood estimate $5$ under a normal model, which is biased downward.
:::

:::Where is the error in Solution B?
The parameter $p$ is a fixed number, so a probability statement about it after the interval has been computed is not what the 95% means. The confidence level is the long-run fraction of intervals, built the same way from repeated samples, that cover $p$. This particular interval either covers it or it does not.
:::

sections.title: Common questions

parts.md: Deviations from the sample mean are systematically smaller than deviations from the true mean, because $\bar X$ is fitted to the same data. Dividing the centred sum of squares by $n-1$ exactly compensates, making $S^2$ unbiased for $\sigma^2$: $E\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2=(n-1)\sigma^2$.
parts.title: Why does the sample variance divide by n − 1?

parts.md: No. A slightly biased estimator can have a smaller mean squared error. The normal-model MLE of the variance is biased but has smaller MSE than $S^2$ (see the simulation). Choose by MSE, not by unbiasedness alone.
parts.title: Is an unbiased estimator always better?

parts.md: Because $\sigma$ is estimated by $S$, which adds uncertainty. The $t$ distribution has heavier tails, so more of the area is far from the centre and the 95% cut-off moves out. As $n$ grows, $t_{0.025,n-1}\to1.96$.
parts.title: Why is the t critical value bigger than 1.96?

parts.md: Enough successes and failures that the normal approximation is reasonable. With very few successes the interval can have much lower coverage than 95%, as the simulation shows for $p=0.05$, $n=30$.
parts.title: What does 'sufficiently large n' mean for the proportion interval?

parts.md: No. For the Bernoulli mean they coincide, but for Uniform$(0,\theta)$ the moment estimate is $2\bar x$ and the likelihood estimate is the sample maximum.
parts.title: Are the method of moments and maximum likelihood estimates always equal?

sections.title: Practice with Python

parts.md:
A coverage simulation shows what “95%” means: the fraction of intervals, over repeated samples, that contain the true parameter. The seed is fixed. The first interval is the approximate proportion interval from this lesson; the second is the t interval for a normal mean. ```html 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
reps = 10_000

def wald_coverage(p, n):
    k = rng.binomial(n, p, reps)
    ph = k / n
    se = np.sqrt(ph * (1 - ph) / n)
    return np.mean((ph - 1.96 * se <= p) & (p <= ph + 1.96 * se))

print("Proportion interval, nominal 95%:")
print("  p=0.20, n=200 :", wald_coverage(0.20, 200))
print("  p=0.05, n=30  :", wald_coverage(0.05, 30), " (few successes: approximation is poor)")

n = 16
x = rng.normal(10, 4, size=(reps, n))
m, s = x.mean(axis=1), x.std(axis=1, ddof=1)
t = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 1)
print("Mean interval, normal data, n=16, nominal 95%:")
print("  t critical value", round(t, 3), "-> coverage", np.mean(np.abs(m - 10) <= t * s / np.sqrt(n)))
print("  using 1.96 instead   -> coverage", np.mean(np.abs(m - 10) <= 1.96 * s / np.sqrt(n)))

Output

Proportion interval, nominal 95%:
  p=0.20, n=200 : 0.9404
  p=0.05, n=30  : 0.7791  (few successes: approximation is poor)
Mean interval, normal data, n=16, nominal 95%:
  t critical value 2.131 -> coverage 0.95
  using 1.96 instead   -> coverage 0.9312
``` Next, a comparison of the two variance estimators for normal data. The MLE divides by $n$ and is biased, but it has a smaller MSE than the unbiased $S^2$: ```html 
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
sigma2, n = 4.0, 5
x = rng.normal(0, 2, size=(200_000, n))        # 200,000 samples of size 5 from N(0, 4)
est = {"MLE, divisor n": x.var(axis=1, ddof=0), "S^2, divisor n-1": x.var(axis=1, ddof=1)}
for name, e in est.items():
    print(f"{name:17s} mean = {e.mean():.3f}  bias = {e.mean() - sigma2:+.3f}  variance = {e.var():.3f}  MSE = {((e - sigma2) ** 2).mean():.3f}")
print("theory: E(MLE) =", (n - 1) / n * sigma2, "  MSE(MLE) =", (2 * n - 1) / n**2 * sigma2**2, "  MSE(S^2) =", 2 * sigma2**2 / (n - 1))

x = np.array([1, 3, 8])
print("data 1, 3, 8: mean", x.mean(), " MLE variance", round(x.var(), 3), " s^2", x.var(ddof=1))

Output

MLE, divisor n    mean = 3.201  bias = -0.799  variance = 5.138  MSE = 5.776
S^2, divisor n-1  mean = 4.001  bias = +0.001  variance = 8.028  MSE = 8.028
theory: E(MLE) = 3.2   MSE(MLE) = 5.76   MSE(S^2) = 8.0
data 1, 3, 8: mean 4.0  MLE variance 8.667  s^2 13.0
```

items.meaning: A parameter is a fixed population quantity; a statistic is a function of the sample; an estimator is a statistic used for a parameter (random); an estimate is its observed value.
B(θ̂) = E(θ̂) − θ. Unbiased means E(θ̂) = θ for every parameter value in the model.
S² = Σ(Xi − X̄)² / (n − 1), unbiased for σ². The normal MLE uses n and is biased by the factor (n − 1)/n.
p̂ ± z·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n), with z = 1.96 for 95%; approximate.

items.term: Confidence interval for a normal mean
items.meaning: x̄ ± t·s/√n with t from the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
The long-run fraction of intervals, built by the procedure over repeated samples, that contain the fixed parameter.
eff(θ̂1, θ̂2) = V(θ̂2) / V(θ̂1) for unbiased estimators; above 1 favours θ̂1. θ̂n is consistent if P(|θ̂n − θ| > ε) → 0 as n → ∞.
Set population moments (functions of the parameters) equal to sample moments and solve.
items.example: Uniform(0, θ): θ/2 = x̄, so θ̂ = 2x̄.

items.meaning: Choose the parameter that maximizes the likelihood of the observed data; usually maximize the log-likelihood.

summary: An estimator is a random statistic; an estimate is its numerical value for the observed sample. Judge an estimator by its sampling distribution: bias, variance and the mean squared error V + bias².
Unbiasedness concerns the centre of the sampling distribution, not the value of a single estimate; a biased estimator can have a smaller MSE.
A 95% confidence interval is a procedure with 95% long-run coverage; for a proportion use p̂ ± z√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n), for a normal mean x̄ ± t·s/√n.
Efficiency compares the variances of unbiased estimators; consistency says that errors become unlikely as n grows.
The method of moments matches population moments to sample moments; maximum likelihood maximizes the likelihood of the observed data. They agree for the Bernoulli but not in general.
The normal-model MLE of the variance divides by n and is biased downward; S² divides by n − 1 and is unbiased.

quiz.title: Check your understanding · Estimation and Confidence Intervals

questions.prompt: The observed values are $x_1=1$, $x_2=3$ and $x_3=5$. What is the sample variance $s^2$, using divisor $n-1$?
questions.explanation: The mean is 3. The squared deviations sum to $4+0+4=8$, so $s^2=8/(3-1)=4$. Dividing by $n=3$ gives $8/3$, and 2 is the standard deviation $s$, not the variance.

questions.prompt: Which equation defines unbiasedness of $\hat\theta$ for $\theta$, for every allowed parameter value?
questions.explanation: Unbiasedness means that the sampling-distribution mean equals the target parameter. It does not require zero variance or zero error in every sample.

questions.prompt: What does a 95% confidence level describe in the frequentist interpretation used in this course?
questions.explanation: The confidence level is the coverage of the interval-construction procedure over repeated samples. A realized interval either contains the fixed parameter or does not.

options.label: A guarantee that any 100 intervals contain the parameter exactly 95 times.
The fraction of observations lying inside each reported interval.
The long-run fraction of intervals that contain the fixed parameter.
A 0.95 probability assigned to the fixed parameter after observing one interval.

questions.prompt: Which procedure describes the method of moments?
questions.explanation: The method of moments equates sample moments with their model-based population counterparts, then solves the resulting parameter equations.

options.label: Choose parameters that make every observation equal to the sample mean.
Minimize the sample size while holding the data fixed.
Always choose the largest observation as the estimate.
Match sample moments to population moments and solve for the parameters.

questions.prompt: For an iid sample with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, use $\hat\mu_n=\bar X+1/n$ to estimate $\mu$. What is its mean square error?
questions.explanation: The bias is $1/n$ and adding a constant leaves the variance at $\sigma^2/n$. The MSE is variance plus squared bias: $\sigma^2/n+1/n^2$.

questions.prompt: An iid normal sample has $n=16$, $\bar x=10$ and $s=4$, with unknown population variance. Using $t_{0.025,15}\approx2.131$, which is the 95% confidence interval for $\mu$?
questions.explanation: The estimated standard error is $s/\sqrt n=4/4=1$. The $t$ interval is $10\pm2.131(1)$, giving the stated endpoints to three decimals. Using $s$ instead of the standard error gives the first option, dividing by $n$ the second, and 1.96 instead of $t$ the third.

questions.prompt: Among 200 iid Bernoulli observations, 40 are successes. Using $z_{0.025}\approx1.96$, which is the textbook's approximate 95% confidence interval for $p$?
questions.explanation: Here $\hat p=0.20$ and $\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat p)=\sqrt{0.20(0.80)/200}\approx0.02828$. The interval is $0.20\pm1.96(0.02828)$, or approximately $[0.145,0.255]$. The first option uses one standard error as the margin instead of 1.96.

questions.prompt: Two unbiased estimators have variances $V(\hat\theta_1)=4$ and $V(\hat\theta_2)=9$. Using the course convention, what is the efficiency of $\hat\theta_1$ relative to $\hat\theta_2$, and which is more precise?
questions.explanation: The defined ratio is $V(\hat\theta_2)/V(\hat\theta_1)=9/4$. The first estimator is more precise because it has the smaller variance; the ratio exceeds one.

questions.prompt: An observed Bernoulli sample has log-likelihood $\ell(p)=8\log p+12\log(1-p)$ for $0\lt p\lt1$. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of $p$?
questions.explanation: Setting $\ell'(p)=8/p-12/(1-p)$ equal to zero gives $8(1-p)=12p$, so $p=8/20=0.40$. The second derivative is negative throughout $(0,1)$. The value $0.60$ swaps successes and failures, and $2/3=8/12$ is an odds ratio.

questions.prompt: A sample from $\text{Uniform}(0,\theta)$, $\theta\gt0$, has observed values $2,4,6$. What is the method-of-moments estimate of $\theta$?
questions.explanation: The population mean is $\theta/2$ and the sample mean is 4. Matching them gives $\hat\theta_{\text{MM}}=2\bar x=8$. The value 4 equates $\theta$ with the mean, and 6 is the sample maximum, which is the MLE rather than the moment estimate.

questions.prompt: Two independent, unbiased estimators $T_1,T_2$ of $\theta$ have variances 4 and 9. For $T_w=wT_1+(1-w)T_2$, which pair gives the variance-minimizing $w\in[0,1]$ and the resulting variance?
questions.explanation: The weighted estimator remains unbiased. Independence gives $V(T_w)=4w^2+9(1-w)^2$. Its derivative is $26w-18$, so the minimum occurs at $w=9/13$, with variance $4(9/13)^2+9(4/13)^2=36/13$. The more precise estimator receives the larger weight.

questions.prompt: Let $K\sim\text{Binomial}(8,p)$ and consider $\tilde p=(K+1)/10$. At $p=0.20$, what is the pair $\big(B(\tilde p),\text{MSE}(\tilde p)\big)$?
questions.explanation: The bias is $(8p+1)/10-p=0.06$. The variance is $8p(1-p)/100=0.0128$, so the MSE is $0.0128+0.06^2=0.0164$. This is below the MSE $p(1-p)/8=0.0200$ of the unbiased estimator $K/8$ at this value of $p$.

questions.prompt: For five iid Bernoulli observations with $0\lt p\lt1$, let $K=\sum_{i=1}^5X_i$. What is $P(X_1=1,X_2=0,X_3=1,X_4=0,X_5=0\mid K=2)$?
questions.explanation: The specified sequence has probability $p^2(1-p)^3$, while $P(K=2)=\binom52p^2(1-p)^3$. Their ratio is $1/\binom52=1/10$, with no remaining dependence on $p$. This illustrates sufficiency of $K$.

questions.prompt: An iid sample from $\text{Uniform}(0,\theta)$ has observed values $2,3,5$. Its likelihood is $L(\theta)=\theta^{-3}$ for $\theta\ge5$ and zero otherwise. Which pair gives the method-of-moments and maximum-likelihood estimates of $\theta$?
questions.explanation: Moment matching uses $\theta/2=\bar x=10/3$, giving $20/3$. The likelihood decreases as $\theta$ increases over the allowed range $[5,\infty)$, so its maximum is at 5. The two estimation methods need not agree.

questions.prompt: An iid sample from a normal population with unknown mean and variance has $n=5$, $\sum_ix_i=10$ and $\sum_ix_i^2=30$. Which triple gives $(\hat\mu_{\text{MLE}},\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}},s^2)$?
questions.explanation: The mean is $10/5=2$ and the centred sum of squares is $30-5(2^2)=10$. Divide by $n$ for the normal-model variance MLE, giving 2, and by $n-1$ for the unbiased sample variance, giving $5/2$. The value 6 is $30/5$ without centring.

questions.prompt: Find the sample variance $s^2$ (divisor $n-1$) of the data $2,4,6,8$. Give an exact fraction or a decimal.
A sample of $n=120$ has 30 successes. Compute the lower endpoint of the approximate 95% confidence interval for $p$ using $z=1.96$. Round to 3 decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\hat p=30/120=0.25$ and $\widehat{\text{SE}}=\sqrt{0.25(0.75)/120}\approx0.03953$. The margin is $1.96\times0.03953\approx0.0775$, so the lower endpoint is $0.25-0.0775=0.1725\approx0.173$ (upper endpoint $0.3275$).

questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a mean is an interval that contains 95% of the individual observations.
questions.explanation: False. The interval is for the population mean, not for individual observations. Individual observations vary by the standard deviation $\sigma$, while the interval's width reflects the much smaller standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

questions.prompt: The maximum-likelihood estimator of the variance of a normal population, with divisor $n$, is unbiased for $\sigma^2$.
questions.explanation: False. $E(\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}})=\tfrac{n-1}n\sigma^2$, so it is biased downward. The sample variance $S^2$ with divisor $n-1$ is unbiased.

questions.prompt: An estimator has bias $0.2$ and variance $0.01$. What is its mean squared error?

lessons.title: Integrated final assessment: choosing the right tool
lessons.description: Eleven scenario questions that mix all three parts — pick the method, justify it, compute it, interpret it.
objectives: Select the mathematical concept that fits a structured data science or machine learning question
Carry the calculation through correctly and interpret the result in context
Spot the classic misreading (wrong sign, standard deviation vs standard error, reversed conditional)
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this assessment you can:
lessons.body:
The final assessment is worth 50% of the course and asks for something different from the topic quizzes: you are given a **situation** and must decide which tool applies, apply it, and say what the answer means. The questions below are a full-length rehearsal covering LO.2–LO.10.

## Choosing the tool

| The question sounds like… | Reach for… | Part |
|---|---|---|
| "How many solutions / can this system be solved?" | Augmented matrix, row reduction, rank | I |
| "Can I undo this transformation?" | Determinant ≠ 0, inverse | I |
| "Which directions does this matrix stretch or preserve?" | Eigenvalues and eigenvectors | I |
| "How fast does the output change when I nudge an input?" | Derivative, chain rule, marginal effect | II |
| "How do I adjust several parameters to lower the loss?" | Gradient, gradient descent | II |
| "How likely is X given that I observed Y?" | Conditional probability, Bayes' rule | III |
| "What is the typical value and spread of a random quantity?" | Expectation, variance | III |
| "How do two quantities move together?" | Covariance, correlation, conditional expectation | III |
| "How much can I trust this sample average?" | Sampling distribution, CLT, standard error, confidence interval | III |

> [!meo] Before computing, write one sentence naming the object you are asked for (a probability, a rate of change, a direction, an interval). Most lost marks come from answering a neighbouring question correctly.

> [!canh-bao] Time yourself: the quiz is built for about 40 minutes. Do the calculations on paper first; the answer check appears only after you commit.
summary: Decide first what is being asked, then choose the method.
Check each result for plausibility: probabilities in [0,1], variances non-negative, descent steps that lower the loss.
The same mathematical objects (matrices, gradients, distributions) appear in every part — the final assessment is about moving between them.

questions.prompt: You fit the line $y=a+bx$ to the points $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,5)$ by solving the normal equations $X^TX\,\beta=X^Ty$ with $\beta=(a,b)^T$. What is the slope $b$? (Give a decimal or a fraction.)
questions.explanation: $X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\6&14\end{bmatrix}$ and $X^Ty=\begin{bmatrix}10\\23\end{bmatrix}$. Row-reduce (or use the inverse, $\det=6$): $a=\tfrac13$, $b=\tfrac32$. Check the residuals: the fitted values $\tfrac{11}{6},\tfrac{20}{6},\tfrac{29}{6}$ are close to $2,3,5$.

questions.prompt: A data set has covariance matrix $\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$. Which statement about the direction of **maximum variance** is correct?
questions.explanation: $\det(\Sigma-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)^2-1=0$ gives $\lambda=3$ and $\lambda=1$. For $\lambda=3$: $(\Sigma-3I)v=0$ gives $v=(1,1)$. The variance along an eigenvector equals its eigenvalue, so the share is $3/(3+1)=75\%$. The equal diagonal entries only mean the two axes have equal variance; the correlation $\Sigma_{12}=1$ tilts the best direction by $45^\circ$.

options.label: It is the eigenvector for the eigenvalue $3$, i.e. the direction $(1,1)/\sqrt2$, and it carries $75\%$ of the total variance.
It is the eigenvector for the eigenvalue $1$, i.e. $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$, and it carries $25\%$ of the total variance.
It is the first coordinate axis $(1,0)$, because $\Sigma_{11}=2$ is the largest diagonal entry.
There is no unique direction, because the two variances are equal.

questions.prompt: The loss is $L(w_1,w_2)=w_1^2+3w_2^2$. Starting at $w=(2,1)$, one gradient-descent step with learning rate $\eta=0.1$ gives which point?
questions.explanation: $\nabla L=(2w_1,\,6w_2)=(4,6)$ at $(2,1)$. Descent moves **against** the gradient: $w\leftarrow w-\eta\nabla L=(2-0.4,\,1-0.6)=(1.6,\,0.4)$. Adding the gradient would climb the hill; using the wrong partial derivative (e.g. $3w_2$ instead of $6w_2$) gives $(1.8,0.7)$.

questions.prompt: The logistic function is $\sigma(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$. What is $\sigma'(0)$?
questions.explanation: By the chain rule $\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\,(1-\sigma(z))$. At $z=0$, $\sigma(0)=\tfrac12$ so $\sigma'(0)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14$. The value $0.5$ is $\sigma(0)$ itself, not its slope.

questions.prompt: A spam filter: $20\%$ of mail is spam. The word "prize" appears in $60\%$ of spam and $10\%$ of non-spam. An email contains "prize". What is $P(\text{spam}\mid\text{prize})$?
questions.explanation: Bayes: $\dfrac{0.6\cdot0.2}{0.6\cdot0.2+0.1\cdot0.8}=\dfrac{0.12}{0.20}=0.60$. $0.12$ is only the numerator (the joint probability); $0.6$ is $P(\text{prize}\mid\text{spam})$, which is a different conditional.

questions.prompt: $X$ has $E[X]=1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=4$. Let $Y=3X-2$. Enter $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$.
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$: the shift $-2$ does not change spread and the factor $3$ is squared, so $9\cdot4=36$. (Also $E[Y]=3\cdot1-2=1$.)

questions.prompt: A sample of $n=100$ values has mean $\bar x=50$ and the population standard deviation is known to be $\sigma=15$. Which is the $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean, and how should it be read?
questions.explanation: The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n=15/10=1.5$, so the margin is $1.96\cdot1.5\approx2.94$ and the interval is $[47.06,52.94]$. $\mu$ is a fixed number; the $95\%$ describes the **procedure**, not this one interval. Using $\sigma=15$ instead of the standard error $1.5$ describes the spread of individual values, not the uncertainty of the mean.

options.label: $[47.06,\ 52.94]$ — if we repeated the sampling many times, about $95\%$ of intervals built this way would contain $\mu$.
$[47.06,\ 52.94]$ — there is a $95\%$ probability that $\mu$ lies in this particular interval.
$[35.0,\ 65.0]$ — the margin is $\sigma$ and the interval does not depend on $n$.

questions.prompt: You flip a coin $10$ times and see $7$ heads. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of the probability of heads?
questions.explanation: The likelihood $p^7(1-p)^3$ is maximised where its derivative of the log vanishes: $7/p-3/(1-p)=0$, so $\hat p=7/10$.

questions.prompt: Observations are i.i.d. with variance $\sigma^2=10$. The estimator $\tilde S^2=\dfrac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2$ is computed from samples of size $n=5$. What is $E[\tilde S^2]$?
questions.explanation: Dividing by $n$ instead of $n-1$ gives $E[\tilde S^2]=\dfrac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2=\dfrac45\cdot10=8$. The estimator is biased low by $2$; dividing by $n-1$ removes the bias.

questions.prompt: If two random variables are uncorrelated ($\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0$), they must be independent.
questions.explanation: False. Independence implies zero covariance, not the other way round. Take $X$ symmetric about $0$ and $Y=X^2$: $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[X^3]-E[X]E[X^2]=0$, yet $Y$ is completely determined by $X$.

questions.prompt: Match each data-science task with the mathematical tool from this course that answers it.

pairs.left: Does a system of equations have a unique solution?
Minimise a differentiable loss over parameters
Probability of a disease given a positive test
Directions a covariance matrix stretches the data most

questions.explanation: Choosing the right tool is learning outcome LO.10. Each pairing follows from the question being asked: existence/uniqueness → rank; "how do I improve parameters" → gradient; reversing a conditional → Bayes; precision of an estimate → standard error; principal directions → eigen-decomposition.
